inputs: Lawfully obtained procurement, payment, grant, corporate-filing, enforcement, and pricing datasets with acquisition dates, source URLs, applicable use rights, immutable snapshots, transformation code, and a documented separation of public records from any authorized nonpublic evidence.

Counsel-defined investigative hypotheses identifying the relevant payment or securities/tax theory, responsible actors, transaction dates, representations, materiality, estimated loss, alternative explanations, and unresolved evidentiary gaps.

Written analytics engagement covering scope, ordinary service fees, conflicts, confidentiality, evidence retention, and ownership; separate counsel assessments of FCA public disclosure, original-source status, first-to-file and limitations issues, SEC original-information requirements, and IRS submission eligibility.
operator_plays.mechanism: Sell scoped B2B forensic-analytics retainers to contingency relator firms, producing reproducible evidence packages for potential False Claims Act matters under 31 U.S.C. §§ 3729–3730 and distinct SEC or IRS whistleblower pathways under 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6 and 26 U.S.C. § 7623. Public-data anomalies alone do not establish a knowingly false, material claim or satisfy Rule 9(b); FCA public-disclosure and original-source analysis differs from the SEC's potential recognition of qualifying independent analysis. Treat service revenue as the operating business and any personally eligible whistleblower award as separate, contingent, potentially multi-year proceeds rather than a purchased claim, promised recovery, or share of counsel's legal fees.
metrics: Collected retainer and milestone revenue minus analyst labor, data licensing, expert review, secure storage, and rework; track receivable days and client concentration without booking speculative awards as earned service revenue.

Evidence quality: reproducible transaction coverage, precision on manually reviewed anomalies, documented alternative explanations, and the share of allegations supported by claim-specific facts rather than aggregate correlations.

Program-specific contingent recovery register: FCA shares generally 15–25% with government intervention or 25–30% without, subject to statutory exceptions; SEC awards generally 10–30% of collected sanctions in qualifying actions exceeding $1 million; IRS § 7623(b) generally 15–30% subject to its monetary, taxpayer-income, and other requirements.
operator_plays.name: Public-Data Forensic Analytics and Relator Litigation-Support Desk

platform_risks.detection_metric: Measure unresolved statutory-element gaps, unsupported claim assertions, source-provenance exceptions, and matters lacking a documented program-specific assessment by counsel.
platform_risks.failure_mode: A compelling statistical pattern is sold as an award-eligible case despite public-disclosure restrictions, insufficient claim-specific facts, or a mismatch between the evidence and the selected whistleblower program.
platform_risks.fallback: Narrow the deliverable to supported forensic findings, preserve exculpatory evidence, and pursue further lawful corroboration only within the engagement; stop unsupported allegations and retain collected service-fee economics separately from any abandoned award thesis.
platform_risks.impact: Dismissal, award denial, wasted litigation expense, confidentiality exposure, and impaired client relationships; paid analytics work does not itself establish relator standing or award eligibility.
platform_risks.trigger: The material is already publicly disclosed or known to authorities, the analyst contributes no qualifying independent analysis or original-source knowledge, or counsel cannot connect anomalies to the required statutory elements.

workflow: 1. Select a narrow, counsel-approved hypothesis and reproduce the underlying transactions from preserved source data; document methodology, false-positive controls, lawful access, and contrary evidence without accessing restricted systems or soliciting privileged material.

2. Build a transaction-level evidence matrix linking alleged conduct to identifiable claims, statements, actors, dates, knowledge indicators, and materiality; have counsel test Rule 9(b) particularity under the governing circuit and assess FCA public-disclosure and original-source issues before characterizing a matter as actionable.

3. Deliver the paid forensic report and reproducible workpapers independently of any award outcome; counsel selects the appropriate pathway, including an FCA complaint initially filed under seal with statutory government disclosures, an SEC TCR submission, or an IRS Form 211, rather than treating the programs as interchangeable.

4. Maintain controlled litigation support, evidence updates, and a docket of counsel-managed deadlines; respect the FCA's initial statutory seal period of at least 60 days and any court-granted extensions, which can extend for years, while forecasting operations from collected retainers rather than expected awards.

chapters.question_prompt: What is the False Claims Act, where did it come from, and what makes a claim legally 'false' and material enough to support a qui tam suit?
chapters.title: The False Claims Act Engine: Origins, Elements, and Economics
chapters.subtitle: Civil War and wartime-fraud roots, materiality and knowledge standards, treble damages and per-claim penalties, the 15–30% relator share, and plain-English primers on qui tam, Stark, and anti-kickback liability
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners across fourteen channels converge on a single engine: a lie connected to a federal dollar, enforced through treble damages, per-claim penalties, and a private relator who keeps 15 to 30 percent of the recovery. Insiders with documents win; outsiders mining PPP data collect closer to 10 percent. Street mechanics center on the sealed complaint, a written disclosure served before filing, a pleading front-loaded with evidence, and a seal that runs 60 days on paper but about 2.5 years in practice, with DOJ averaging 11 months to decide intervention. Recoveries hit $6.8B in FY2025 alongside a record 1,297 qui tam filings. Practitioners split on the knowledge standard, how harshly first-to-file cuts out later relators, per-claim penalty figures, and whether policy-driven false certifications belong in the Act at all.

key_metrics.label: Relator Share of Government Recovery
key_metrics.value: 15% to 30% of whatever the government recovers
key_metrics.context: Hamilton and Newman state the whistleblower is entitled to 15 to 30 percent of recovery through settlement or judgment; public-information outsider cases such as PPP data mining pay about 10 percent.

key_metrics.label: Per-Claim Penalty on Top of Treble Damages
key_metrics.metric: Per-Claim Penalty on Top of Treble Damages
key_metrics.value: $13,000 to $27,000 per claim plus 3x the claim value
key_metrics.context: Penalty stack quoted by Hamilton and Newman; courts reject excessive-fines defenses, and an 11th Circuit urine-testing case turned single-digit-thousand losses into about $1M on appeal.

key_metrics.label: DOJ Intervention Decision Time
key_metrics.value: About 11 months across all cases
key_metrics.context: Current average time for intervention decisions reported on the Phillips & Cohen panel, against a statutory seal that starts at 60 days.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner reduces the Act to the same core. Maryanne Hamilton and Darth Newman frame a case as "a lie that's connected to a federal dollar" and list five elements to prove: claim, falsity, knowledge, materiality, and damages, meaning the claim was actually paid [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:03:41]. The federal dollar can sit anywhere down the waterfall, so subcontractor claims to a prime contractor and block grants passed through states still qualify. The Brown, LLC practitioner draws the hard line on payer: overbilling a private insurer or a self-pay patient is not an FCA case, while overbilling Medicare or Medicaid is [3ugChIElhkM @ 00:00:56]. Michael Rosenblat compresses the screen into two tests anyone can run: the government must be the victim, meaning it lost money or would have refused the bill had it known the truth, and the conduct must be fraud rather than a mere breach of contract [8iceOOTBGds @ 00:00:57]. Katie Fink at OIG lists the bread-and-butter schemes that clear both tests: services not rendered, duplicate claims, upcoding, and claims unsupported by the medical record, plus referrals that violate the Anti-Kickback statute or Stark law, which turn otherwise clean bills into false claims [BbZ78QTLztQ @ 00:00:22]. Insiders who see these patterns daily are the raw material of the whole engine.

The knowledge bar sits lower than most targets assume. Mark Kleiman reads the statute as "very specific in saying that intent to defraud is not required," with reckless disregard and deliberate indifference enough, which in practice works out to "pretty much a gross negligence standard" [yN7NRjwYKFs @ 00:31:35]. Hamilton's scienter fact pattern is the one that keeps surfacing in real files: a biller objects and is told "just do it that way. That's how we get paid," and the same speakers stress the Act is not a negligence statute and does not require intent to defraud [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:19:41]. The exposure stack is what makes the engine run. Treble damages land on top of a per-claim penalty, and for healthcare providers each separate request for payment or code on a billing statement may be considered a claim, which "can quickly add up to a significant liability"; Quimbee adds expulsion from Medicare to the civil menu and flags a 2015 judgment above $237M [1SUxz8N7UU8 @ 00:00:56]. The Phillips & Cohen panel states that once the government intervenes, for many defendants "it's simply going to be game over," because penalties this severe compel settlement even when the defense believes it holds strong arguments [5-ptDaAQkvI @ 00:10:41]. That asymmetry is why intervention is the prize every relator chases.

On who wins and what they collect, the consensus is tight and repeatable. Hamilton and Newman prefer insiders because they bring documents, photos, and sometimes recordings, and the FBI may wire a relator; outsiders, data miners, patients, and competitors can file too, but public-information outsider cases such as PPP data mining pay about 10% rather than 15 to 30%, and some lawyers avoid them entirely [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:29:41]. The Brown, LLC practitioner agrees insiders are best, says patients filing is "a lot harder," and tells outsiders to build their file through former employees and other patients [3ugChIElhkM @ 00:02:35]. The share band is consistent across the board: 15 to 30% of whatever the government recovers, by settlement or judgment, with Andrew Jonathan Hillman splitting it into 15 to 25% when the government intervenes and 25 to 30% when it declines [AcMsQCQm5QI @ 00:02:32]. Melissa Green Law Group lists the baseline prerequisites for a viable case: a specific false claim, information that is original, and a whistleblower who is first to file, with the decision to report internally first capable of changing the outcome. Retaliation remedies round out the floor: reinstatement, double back pay plus interest, and additional compensation [Lbcq9qvdJtE @ 00:02:37].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The filing sequence is where cases are won or lost before a judge ever sees them. The Phillips & Cohen panel teaches a strict order: serve the written disclosure statement with all the material evidence before filing the complaint, which preserves original-source status, then file in camera with service on the Attorney General and the local U.S. Attorney's Office [5-ptDaAQkvI @ 00:18:37]. Venue under §1391 is chosen on USAO trust, aggressiveness, and resources, and on favorable circuit law. Kleiman runs a tighter pre-filing play: pick up the phone and talk to an AUSA in civil frauds or send an email about two weeks before filing to lock in original-source credit, then deliver the disclosure statement on a flash drive with the memo to follow [yN7NRjwYKFs @ 01:21:07]. GBB Legal attacks the pleading itself, warning that too many lawyers file a complaint and wait to see what comes after; the move is to gather as much evidence as quickly as possible and front-load it into the complaint, building for a jury from day one and stacking circumstantial building blocks because defendants deliberately avoid creating direct evidence [FAfnVdZ6Ie0 @ 00:01:11]. Cory Reiss adds the gag rule: publicly available information disqualifies a relator, so keep the allegations to yourself instead of broadcasting them to the media [7-9Z8vNWVFc @ 00:01:51].

Once filed, the clock runs far past the statute's 60 days. The Brown, LLC practitioner reports the government "always literally always" wants more time and applies for extensions, with seals running 5 to 7-plus years at the long end and averaging about two and a half years [3ugChIElhkM @ 00:06:49]. Hamilton and Newman log an initial government interview within 1 to 3 months, a fastest seal of 12 months, a longest of 10 years, and call 2 to 3 years "the good side of average," with 5 years not unexpected [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:35:15]. The Phillips & Cohen panel puts the current intervention-decision average across all cases at about 11 months, and notes a full case can stack 3 to 6 years of lookback on a 2 to 3 year investigation, leaving witnesses recalling events roughly a decade old. The relator is not idle during the seal: the job is finding documents, explaining company lingo, locating witnesses and flagging them friendly or hostile, and underwriting expert costs. Relators who are not ready to litigate after a declination quietly welcome every extension [5-ptDaAQkvI @ 00:37:27]. Against The Fraud puts the federal intervention rate under 25% of cases, with FBI and postal inspectors doing the investigative legwork [QmB-gKtr0tc @ 00:06:14].

The money math is where the engine pays out. Hamilton and Newman quote 13 to $27,000 per claim on top of three times the value of the claim, note that defendants pay the relator's attorney fees even when they settle, and describe an 11th Circuit urine-testing case where losses in the single-digit thousands, at roughly $15 per Medicare urine test, became about $1M on appeal [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:23:57]. They also show the declination trap in dollars: a $500K expert bill against a $1M theft where the relator's share would land around $150K. Kleiman reports that treble damages usually settle at 2x to 2.5x, that penalties of $11.5K to $23K per claim trigger fights over how claims are counted, and that fee petitions should go in Excel with no block billing and an expected 10 to 15% haircut. Kleiman also pegs the government's return at $14 to $15, up to $30, for every $1 of enforcement [yN7NRjwYKFs @ 00:06:57]. Against The Fraud runs the headline math: a $100M settlement at the 15 to 30% band yields up to $30M, against an FY2025 haul of $6.8B, over $5.3B of it from qui tam [QmB-gKtr0tc @ 00:07:31]. Andrew Jonathan Hillman logs a record 1,297 qui tam suits filed that year [AcMsQCQm5QI @ 00:01:16].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split on the street is the knowledge bar. Amanda Lockaby tells prospective relators that the key is demonstrating intentional fraud and that mistakes or negligence are not enough [OfdepsSYjp4 @ 00:01:29]. Mark Kleiman runs the opposite playbook. In his reading the statute says intent to defraud is not required, reckless disregard and deliberate indifference are enough, and in practice the bar sits near gross negligence [yN7NRjwYKFs @ 00:31:35]. Maryanne Hamilton and Darth Newman side with Kleiman. They frame the Act as no negligence statute that also carries no intent-to-defraud requirement, and their classic proof is a biller who objects and is told "just do it that way. That's how we get paid" [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:19:55]. Andrew Hillman reads the knowingly definition the same way, folding in deliberate ignorance and reckless disregard, and states that no proof of specific intent to defraud is required [AcMsQCQm5QI @ 00:01:54]. The split drives intake screening. A Lockaby-style intake rejects sloppy-billing files that a Kleiman-style intake pushes forward when the paper trail shows someone was warned and kept billing anyway. Teams on the reckless-disregard threshold work a wider pipeline of files built on warnings that were ignored. Teams anchored on intentional fraud run a narrower docket and pass on cases built only on carelessness.

Money splits are the second fault line. Against The Fraud pitches a flat 15 to 30 percent and treats first-to-file as winner-take-all. Later relators get nothing, it is a literal race to the DOJ, and absolute urgency is required [QmB-gKtr0tc @ 00:08:17]. Kleiman describes a softer market. Shares run 15 to 25 percent on intervened cases and 25 to 30 percent on declined ones, mostly by negotiation. The first relator commonly keeps 85 to 90 percent, so a later filer still carves out a slice [yN7NRjwYKFs @ 01:24:16]. Brown, LLC splits the difference. With full overlap the later filer is out and the first filer has no duty to share, though parties sometimes negotiate an arrangement anyway. Non-overlapping claims, such as back braces in one complaint and injections in another, can both proceed [3ugChIElhkM @ 00:11:57]. Cory Reiss quotes the intervened band as "15 to 20 25%", depending on how helpful the information was, rising to as much as 30 percent once a declined case unseals [7-9Z8vNWVFc @ 00:02:28]. The operator has to pick a lane. One option is to sprint and file early to lock priority under the race model. The other is to file a tighter, non-overlapping theory and negotiate a split if a rival relator surfaces later.

Timelines diverge just as hard. Hamilton and Newman have seen seals last 12 months at the fastest and 10 years at the longest. They call 2 to 3 years the good side of average and say 5 years is not unexpected [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:36:19]. Brown, LLC pegs the average at about two and a half years and reports that the government literally always wants more time to investigate [3ugChIElhkM @ 00:07:08]. Michael Granston puts DOJ's intervention decision at about 11 months across all cases. Relator counsel on the same panel concede that relators who are not ready to litigate after a declination quietly welcome extensions [5-ptDaAQkvI @ 00:37:27]. A second strategic split runs through the Fraud in America panel. Jessica Tilman separates core fraud from policy-driven false certifications, warns that weak cases weaken the law, and points to contract remedies. Sarah Frasier counters that cases turn on lying, cheating, or stealing, and cites short-shelf food shipped to Kuwait [lX4p0oRMWls @ 00:33:01]. Nimish Desai adds that big contractors run creative cost accounting and ROI calculations. Operators budget cash for a multi-year seal and decide early which kind of file they hold. A core-theft case is one thing. A certification theory is another, because it is exposed to policy reversals like the DEI clause reversal Tilman described.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is a case that dies on materiality after years of work. Hamilton describes an egregious file where the agency said, in effect, we'd pay it anyway, and the case died about two years in. The working rule is that out-of-spec military parts are material and wrong-color parts probably are not [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:21:22]. Declination economics bite next. Against The Fraud reports that DOJ intervenes in under 25 percent of cases and holds Granston-memo dismissal power [QmB-gKtr0tc @ 00:06:14]. Hamilton and Newman walk through a declined matter where a $500K expert bill stood against a $1M theft, leaving a relator share of about $150K [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:39:22]. Brown, LLC litigates many declined cases but drops them when the government finds no fraud, so a declination paired with a negative finding ends the file [3ugChIElhkM @ 00:07:30]. The economics check runs on three questions before money is committed. Would the payer actually stop paying if it knew the truth? Does the damages pool clear expert cost with room left for a meaningful share? Does the theory still hold up after a declination? A file that fails any one of them gets triaged out before the seal clock starts consuming capital and the relator's patience.

Leaks and lost priority are the second cluster. Brown, LLC warns that a former biller approached as a co-relator may refuse and then file first. Collaborators therefore have to be trusted, and the complaint should be as near to finished as possible before that call. Because there is no index of sealed cases, firms have learned years later that they were second to fourth in line, and the government sometimes sits on that knowledge [3ugChIElhkM @ 00:10:17]. Reiss flags the self-inflicted version. Publicly available information disqualifies a relator, so keep the facts to yourself instead of broadcasting them to the media [7-9Z8vNWVFc @ 00:01:51]. Kleiman adds that even a FOIA response counts as public disclosure. To protect original-source status, he says to pick up the phone or email an AUSA in civil frauds about two weeks before filing [yN7NRjwYKFs @ 01:21:07]. The Phillips & Cohen panel locks in the sequence. Serve the written disclosure statement with all the material evidence before the complaint goes in, then file in camera with service on the AG and the local USAO [5-ptDaAQkvI @ 00:18:37]. Three or four cases against the same defendant are now common. Every day between spotting a scheme and serving disclosure gives a rival relator, a talkative witness, or a records request another chance to erase the claim.

The final trap set is personal exposure. Brown, LLC tells relators to think about how dirty their hands are before starting. Some involvement is normal. Masterminding the scheme, profiting from it, or delaying the report drastically cuts the award, and egregious involvement could end in arrest [3ugChIElhkM @ 00:10:00]. Kleiman narrows the hard bar to someone who planned and initiated the fraud and cites a GE relator who still collected 22.5 percent. He also warns that Nassar but-for causation is a drawback on the federal retaliation claim, which is why he files timely state claims [yN7NRjwYKFs @ 01:00:34]. Frasier reports that negotiating with the company, even in a small way, brings a release, and calls that a key reason to talk to a qui tam lawyer early [lX4p0oRMWls @ 00:42:28]. Kleiman's counter-move is that a release of all claims with a 1542 waiver still lets the FCA case proceed. A certification that no FCA case was filed, however, is a deal breaker. Hamilton and Newman close the loop on secrecy. Anonymity carries a non-zero chance of being outed, and that risk stays live for the full length of a seal that can run for years [HocnawRgrAA @ 00:56:25]. Operators price culpability, release language, and identity exposure before the first government interview.

callout.title: Four Kill-Switch Checks Before the Complaint Goes Under Seal
callout.body: Every item below is a pitfall practitioners report losing cases, priority, or award share to. A file that fails any one is fixed or dropped before filing.
items: Materiality check: confirm the defect is the kind the payer would refuse to pay for, as with out-of-spec military parts, not wrong-color parts [Justia — HocnawRgrAA @ 00:23:01].

Disclosure sequencing: serve the written disclosure statement with all material evidence before filing the complaint to preserve original-source status [Phillips & Cohen LLP — 5-ptDaAQkvI @ 00:18:37].
Silence discipline: keep the facts to yourself instead of broadcasting them to the media, because public information disqualifies a relator [Shipman Wright Law — 7-9Z8vNWVFc @ 00:01:51].

Dirty-hands audit: measure your own involvement first, because masterminding, profiting, or delaying the report drastically reduces the award [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 3ugChIElhkM @ 00:10:00].

chapters.question_prompt: How does a would-be relator build a case strong enough for a whistleblower firm to take on contingency and for DOJ to pursue?
chapters.title: Relator Intake: Selecting, Building, and Filing a Winning Qui Tam
chapters.subtitle: How firms screen cases, non-employee and participant relators, first-to-file and public-disclosure traps, evidence gathering mistakes, contingency fees, sealed complaints and partial seal lifts, and how to report Medicare and customs fraud to counsel first
chapters.executive_summary: Qui tam intake practitioners converge on one operating rule: stay silent, get to experienced counsel, and file first. Levin Papantonio and Brown, LLC warn that going public forfeits original-source status and invites a rival filer to block the line. Beasley Allen, Sanford Heisler Sharp McKnight, and Chapman Law Group require firsthand, verifiable knowledge pleaded with who, what, when, where, and how. Brown, LLC underwrites cases above $10 million in actual pre-trebling damages on a sliding scale against proof strength, rejects difficult clients, and scrutinizes outsider data-mining cases built from ProPublica PPP records or competitor customs intelligence harder than insider cases. Relator shares run 15 to 30 percent, fees are contingent, and seals renew 6 months at a time, with Stephen Teller reporting many cases closing two or three years after filing. Teller also warns against running documents through AI before calling counsel.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Silence before filing is the first rule every intake lawyer hammers. James Kaufman at Levin Papantonio tells relators flatly not to go to the newspaper or the press, because publishing the information strips its value to the government and risks blowing the public disclosure bar, at which point the relator is no longer the original source [xH5IpDAiP5c @ 00:00:36]. The same team ties that to first-to-file: going public raises the odds someone else files first and blocks the relator in line, and host Peter Muggie calls the urge to shout it from the rooftops the absolute worst thing a relator can do [xH5IpDAiP5c @ 00:01:36]. Jason T. Brown of Brown, LLC repeats the race logic at the close of the firm's case-selection breakdown, warning that the first whistleblower to file generally blocks everyone behind them and that another day someone else may file the case [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:09:15]. Brown also says the worst thing a whistleblower can do is act impulsively, talk to the wrong person, or expose themselves before knowing their rights [Cz4DaWsS-xM @ 00:05:25]. The firm extends that discipline to the internet: case-specific questions about a real-life scenario should never be left publicly in comments, because doing so can only compromise the case, so relators should email or call counsel privately instead [N4uuM9uvRYY @ 00:06:35].

The second point of agreement is that a relator must hold firsthand, provable knowledge, not a hunch. Beasley Allen states that to be a whistleblower you have to have some first-hand knowledge about what is actually occurring, and notes the typical relator is a bookkeeper, a nurse, or someone dealing directly with services involving the federal government [dnDB-BkTNpk @ 00:01:01]. Sanford Heisler Sharp McKnight frames it as knowledge plus traceability: the whistleblower must trace the wrongdoing in a way that is believable, credible, and verifiable, whether through documents, emails, internal traffic discussing how dangerous the scheme is, or superior knowledge [zvfb6_cVFWg @ 00:02:37]. Brown, LLC asks first whether the caller is an insider or an outsider, defining the insider as someone who saw the meetings, has the emails, and can point to where the bodies are buried, adding that insiders usually clear the public disclosure bar while outsiders often do not [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:01:45]. Ron Chapman of Chapman Law Group lands on the same pleading reality: because fraud is so easy to allege, the relator must supply the what, when, where, how, and who, and the relator's most important job is producing enough facts for a disclosure statement [4cRTBx7ikiY @ 00:03:08].

Third, every practitioner agrees the economics run on government money, contingency, and secrecy. Tony Munter of Price Benowitz reduces a good case to two elements: it must plainly scream out as fraud, and some government agency must have lost money, because a wild fraud between two securities firms without government money is not a traditional False Claims Act case [IX4WhZTmPRI @ 00:01:07]. Munter also explains why contingency is the only workable fee model: the relator pays nothing up front, even after being fired with no money, and since the sealed case can be discussed with no one except counsel, the relator has to marry the lawyer and cannot be worrying that every phone call costs money [KMtkKgsZzRo @ 00:00:43]. Cohen Milstein confirms the seal mechanics, stating that only the whistleblower, counsel, the court, and the government know a case has been filed, and that the firm works fully contingent, collecting a fee only when the relator receives an award [skGozAS0va8 @ 00:00:39]. Gary Martin Hays walks the same sequence for a Medicare billing specialist being told to bill for services never performed: find a lawyer, have the attorney research the evidence, file under seal so even the defendant is kept in the dark, then let the Department of Justice investigate and decide whether to intervene [64dIGOXUwoc @ 00:05:05].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Brown, LLC runs intake like an underwriting desk. Jason T. Brown says the firm turns down the overwhelming majority of cases and has said no to millions of dollars in offered fees, because a whistleblower case is a years-long war [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:00:00]. The damages screen is explicit: as a general rule the firm wants fraud against the government exceeding $10 million in actual damages, measured pre-trebling, against a solvent defendant, but damages and liability sit on a sliding scale, so a billion-dollar fraud can justify hard proof problems while a smaller case with a smoking-gun document can beat a giant case built on inference [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:02:58]. The third filter is where most cases die: facts versus theories. 'I think my company is defrauding Medicare' is a call; patient files, billing codes, dates, and the director's email ordering upcoding is a case, because Rule 9B particularity gets complaints dismissed every week [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:04:15]. The remaining filters are character, geography, and program: the firm refuses callers who are mean to intake staff or demand to speak only with Brown, weighs circuit splits and how aggressive each United States Attorneys Office is, and concentrates on bounty programs. Stephen Teller's first move is simpler: have the insider describe exactly how the government is getting ripped off [SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:04:16].

Building the package is document-driven. Stephen Teller of Teller Law asks the insider to describe the fraud, then gathers whatever paper or electronic records help explain it and drafts a couple of long letters plus a complaint that fits the False Claims Act, all handed to the Department of Justice and filed under seal without serving the defendant [SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:04:32]. Ron Chapman shows what the disclosure statement should carry using incident-to billing: a practice can bill 100 percent for a nurse practitioner or physician assistant who would normally draw 85 percent, but only if the physician is present in the office, so a biller who sees the doctor managing staff by telephone or text message has a scheme worth documenting [4cRTBx7ikiY @ 00:03:41]. The statement then gets built from calendars, billing records, medical records, and a list of people with intimate knowledge who might testify, because the US attorney uses it to decide whether to intervene [4cRTBx7ikiY @ 00:04:34]. Brown, LLC adds the construction rules: build a timeline, separate what you know from what you suspect, identify who directed the conduct, preserve lawful evidence already in your possession, and never destroy, alter, or hide anything or take privileged or unauthorized documents [CZeUV80NaAA @ 00:07:40].

Once filed, the clock is slow and the seal is the operating environment. Teller reports the seal typically runs 6 months at a time, with the government asking the judge for more, so cases stay sealed 8 months, 14 months, or a couple of years, and many Teller Law cases finish two or three years after filing; even the fast ones take almost a year [SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:08:23]. During that window the Department of Justice contacts the client agency, issues civil investigative demands for documents, written answers, or depositions, and occasionally has relators wear recording devices [SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:09:24]. At the end of the seal the government intervenes or declines; frequently it has already negotiated a settlement, intervenes, and the case is dismissed, while a declined case can still be litigated by the relator, sometimes over government opposition. Brown, LLC describes the partial seal lift that often precedes settlement: the government asks the relator and counsel to consent to sharing a redacted complaint with the defendant to hear its position, and even without consent the judge typically defers to the government as the true party of interest [N4uuM9uvRYY @ 00:03:00]. Brown adds that experienced defense counsel start suspecting a hidden case when government demands keep circling the same subject [N4uuM9uvRYY @ 00:05:09].

callout.title: Intake Moves the Practitioners Actually Teach
callout.body: Four field-level moves that protect the claim and sharpen the pitch before counsel files under seal.
items: Do not run your documents through AI or write your own summary before calling counsel; it raises confidentiality concerns and can create discovery problems [Stephen Teller - Teller Law — SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:06:42]

Do not self-reject because the number feels small: tell the firm the number, how you got there, and show the proof, and let counsel do the math [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:04:01]

If you are also being retaliated against, do not settle that case carelessly, because it can accidentally settle the False Claims Act case out from under the government [Stephen Teller - Teller Law — SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:06:26]

Outsider patients can corroborate with online complaints from others, top-prescriber status, and public-record proof that the doctor owns the supply clinic [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 39Q-yYGWPVg @ 00:06:35]

sop_steps.title: Lock Down Silence and Privilege
sop_steps.action: Tell no press, HR, boss, or regulator; call qui tam counsel first.
sop_steps.detail: A call to a lawyer is privileged even if you never sign a retainer, so you can ask whether you are in trouble before taking any other step [Sanford Heisler Sharp McKnight — zvfb6_cVFWg @ 00:01:55]

sop_steps.title: Score Your Own Exposure
sop_steps.action: Answer what you did, what you knew, when you knew it, and which program applies.
sop_steps.detail: Brown, LLC flips the strategy to protection the moment the relator's own conduct could be questioned, using four questions plus whether the relator received money from the fraud [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — CZeUV80NaAA @ 00:01:14]

sop_steps.title: Assemble the Disclosure Statement
sop_steps.action: Build who, what, when, where, and how from calendars, billing records, medical records, and witnesses.
sop_steps.detail: Counsel turns the relator's facts into the disclosure statement the US attorney uses to decide whether to intervene [Chapman Law Group: Health Care Attorneys — 4cRTBx7ikiY @ 00:04:34]

sop_steps.title: File Under Seal and Ride the Extensions
sop_steps.action: File the complaint with DOJ under seal and plan for repeated 6-month extensions.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split among these practitioners is over who actually gets to be a relator. Jason T. Brown of Brown, LLC opens intake by sorting insiders from outsiders: an employee, billing manager, or compliance officer who saw the meetings and holds the emails usually clears the public disclosure bar, while outsiders often do not and get underwritten far more skeptically [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:02:26]. Yet in a separate session the same firm stresses that nowhere in the False Claims Act does a relator need to be an employee, listing board members, consultants, patients, data miners, statistics quants, and competitors as live categories [39Q-yYGWPVg @ 00:01:00]. Beasley Allen draws the line tighter, insisting a relator must hold first-hand knowledge of what is actually occurring, and says the typical relator is a bookkeeper, a nurse, or someone dealing directly with services involving the federal government [dnDB-BkTNpk @ 00:01:01]. The outsider lane stays open but narrow: Brown points to PPP cases built by cross-checking ProPublica headcount and revenue against corporate filings, yet says entities formed solely to litigate on prescribing-propensity data drew backlash, and the firm wants to see a little bit of the flame, not just smoke, before it signs on [39Q-yYGWPVg @ 00:08:24].

The second fault line is how much the relator should do before counsel is engaged. Ron Chapman of Chapman Law Group describes the insider actively looking around, gathering information, and assembling calendars, billing records, medical records, and lists of willing witnesses that the attorney turns into a disclosure statement [4cRTBx7ikiY @ 00:04:34]. Brown pushes the opposite way: do not go gather documents on your own, and confirm with an attorney that you have lawful, ethical access before forwarding anything [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:04:28]. Elsewhere, Brown warns that the instinct to gather evidence gets people fired for probing around, or criminally charged for touching information they had no lawful right to access [Cz4DaWsS-xM @ 00:06:48]. Stephen Teller adds a modern wrinkle: do not run your documents through AI or have it build a summary before calling the lawyer, because it raises confidentiality concerns and can create discovery problems later [SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:06:42]. The practical synthesis is sequencing. Chapman's document-heavy playbook and Teller's intake, where the client describes the fraud and then starts gathering paper and electronic records with counsel, both work once a lawyer is already steering what is collected and how. Get the order wrong and, as Brown puts it, the wrong first move can make a bad situation worse.

Practitioners also split on which cases are worth the war. Brown runs a hard filter: the firm generally wants fraud above $10 million in actual, pre-trebling damages, a solvent defendant, and a sliding scale where a smoking-gun document can carry a smaller case while a billion-dollar fraud can justify hard proof problems [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:03:29]. Tony Munter reduces selection to two questions: does the case plainly scream fraud, and can you name the government agency that lost money, with public disclosure, original source, and limitations issues treated as important but secondary to that core [IX4WhZTmPRI @ 00:00:51]. On fees there is no real dispute about structure, only emphasis. Munter calls the contingent fee the only way to run these cases because the seal leaves the relator with one person to call and nobody should ration phone calls to counsel [KMtkKgsZzRo @ 00:01:37]. Brown frames the same contingency as the reason for selectivity, since the firm funds every case with its own money and years. Cohen Milstein likewise only receives a fee if the client receives a whistleblower reward. On timing, Teller says the longer the better, because a long seal means the government believes the case is worth the effort, while even fast cases run almost a year [SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:12:14].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The fastest way to kill a qui tam is to go loud. Levin Papantonio's James Kaufman says the urge to get the word out can blow the case: going to the newspaper or press dumps the information into the public, strips its value to the government, and risks the public disclosure bar that ends original-source status [xH5IpDAiP5c @ 00:00:36]. The panel calls it counterintuitive: the instinct to shout it to the rooftops to save people money or get them out of harm's way is the absolute worst thing you could do. Publicity also raises the odds that someone else files first and blocks the relator in line. Brown frames the same clock bluntly: the first whistleblower to file generally blocks everyone behind them, and another day someone else may file your case [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:09:15]. Seal discipline continues after filing. Munter warns that once a case is under seal the relator cannot tell anyone except the lawyer, which is why Munter says you have to marry your lawyer at that point [KMtkKgsZzRo @ 00:01:03]. Brown adds that posting case-specific questions in public comments can only compromise the case, and that experienced defense counsel will start suspecting a hidden False Claims Act action once government demands keep circling the same subject [N4uuM9uvRYY @ 00:06:35].

Relators with dirty hands face a different failure mode. Brown says big sources bring big problems, and that once a whistleblower's own conduct can be questioned the strategy flips from chasing an award to protection. Under the False Claims Act, a relator who planned and initiated the violation can see the award reduced, and one convicted of criminal conduct arising from it is dismissed from the civil action and receives nothing [CZeUV80NaAA @ 00:02:12]. The biggest misconception Brown flags is immunity: a whistleblower submission is not an immunity agreement, and the reward track and the criminal cooperation track are two different things that can overlap and sometimes conflict [CZeUV80NaAA @ 00:05:24]. Brown's six-rung ladder runs from minimal involvement through knowing participant, manager or approver, planner or initiator, and finally obstruction, meaning destroyed evidence, altered records, lies, or interference with investigators, with exposure rising at every rung and with every dollar of direct benefit. Teller flags a quieter version of the trap: settle a related retaliation claim carelessly and the relator might accidentally settle the False Claims Act case out from under the government, though Teller says it is rare [SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:06:26]. Brown adds that HR will ask why the employee waited a year or two and treat that delay as grounds for termination [Cz4DaWsS-xM @ 00:07:46].

Past the publicity trap, cases fail on proof and on the relator. Brown says the facts-versus-theories gap is where most cases die: a caller who thinks the company is defrauding Medicare has a theory, while patient files, billing codes, dates, and the director's email ordering upcoding make a case, and courts dismiss complaints every week under Rule 9B when the relator is strong on suspicion and weak on specifics [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:04:41]. Chapman makes the same point from the healthcare side, calling the disclosure statement extremely important because the US attorney uses it to decide whether to intervene [4cRTBx7ikiY @ 00:04:48]. Credibility is the second filter. Brown says the government vets the whistleblower before it vets the defendant, that a shifting story or a vendetta will be felt by a jury and by the Department of Justice, and that the firm has walked away from probably hundreds of millions in potential fees over difficult clients, including callers rude to intake staff [Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:05:56]. The economics are unforgiving. Brown says more cases fail than succeed even after the firm takes them, and Teller says even fast cases take almost a year, with seals renewed six months at a time, and quite a few of Teller's cases finish two or three years after filing [SiATzxJHy2Y @ 00:08:23].

callout.title: Four Kill Switches To Clear Before Any Qui Tam Filing
callout.body: Every item below is a pitfall practitioners report sinking relators before the government ever reads the complaint. Clear all four before moving records, talking to anyone at work, or contacting a regulator.
items: Silence check: no newspaper, no press, no public posts, no case-specific questions in comment sections; going public kills original-source status and invites a first-to-file block [Levin Papantonio — xH5IpDAiP5c @ 00:00:36].

Exposure check: answer what you actually did, what you knew, when you knew it, and which program applies, then follow the dough on any money you received [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — CZeUV80NaAA @ 00:01:14].

Lawful access check: the government will ask how you knew and whether you lawfully accessed the information; you cannot illegally access information you were not entitled to [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 39Q-yYGWPVg @ 00:03:55].

Government money check: without some element of government money and an identifiable agency that lost it, you do not have a traditional False Claims Act case [Tony Munter Attorney at Law — IX4WhZTmPRI @ 00:01:46].

chapters.pull_quote: If you can't explain how somebody got ripped off, then there's a good chance the case won't work out. Attributed to Tony Munter Attorney at Law (IX4WhZTmPRI @ 00:00:51).
action_checklist: Call a whistleblower lawyer before telling anyone at work; the conversation is privileged even if you never sign a retainer, so ask whether you are in trouble [Sanford Heisler Sharp McKnight — zvfb6_cVFWg @ 00:01:55].

Build a timeline, separate what you know from what you suspect, identify who directed the conduct and what documents exist, and never destroy, alter, or hide anything [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — CZeUV80NaAA @ 00:07:40].

Assemble the what, when, where, how, and who of the fraud so counsel can draft a disclosure statement with intricate facts and details [Chapman Law Group: Health Care Attorneys — 4cRTBx7ikiY @ 00:03:08].
Do not self-reject on size: tell the firm the damages number, how you got there, and show the proof so they can do the math [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — Hb6Ogl9Fm8I @ 00:04:01].
Name the government agency that lost money and be ready to explain in plain terms how it got ripped off [Tony Munter Attorney at Law — IX4WhZTmPRI @ 00:01:46].
Retain counsel on contingency and keep every conversation about the sealed case between you and your lawyer only [Tony Munter Attorney at Law — KMtkKgsZzRo @ 00:01:03].

chapters.question_prompt: What actually happens to a qui tam after filing—through intervention, litigation, settlement, or dismissal—and what do relators experience along the way?
chapters.title: Inside the Qui Tam Lifecycle: Intervention, Litigation, Settlement, and Dismissal
chapters.subtitle: Post-Escobar materiality fights, recurring litigation issues, ethics of relator investigations and interviews, multi-relator and competitor/analyst/Doe relators, settlement negotiation, the spike in government 4731(c)(2)(A) dismissals, constitutionality challenges, and the USIS dumping case study
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree the qui tam lifecycle is won or lost under seal. The 60-to-90-day statutory window routinely stretches past 120 days and sometimes to about five years. DOJ intervenes in only 21 to 24 percent of cases, and a declination reflects cost rather than merits. Street mechanics center on a privilege screen before any document reaches the government, targeted evidence instead of folder grabs, and 'boxed fruit' packages of evidence, draft subpoenas, and org charts. The numbers are concrete: $11,665 to $22,331 per claim on top of treble damages, 15 to 30 percent relator shares, and DOJ dismissals climbing from about 6 to about 25 a year. Mediators settle release scope before money and keep fees out of lump-sum offers. Relator counsel split roughly 50/50 on whether to negotiate fees alongside the merits.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner treats the seal as the opening battlefield of the qui tam lifecycle. Amanda Roach of the Colorado U.S. Attorney's Office describes a seal of at least 60 days that serves three purposes. Partial lifts are available, and under a Fourth Circuit rule a relator may discuss the allegations but not the action [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:40:25]. Rich Hayes, EDNY Civil Deputy Chief, says 60 days is 'not a lot of time to figure out whether there's been a multi-billion dollar fraud perpetrated against the government.' He also reports that courts are allowing less time to decide intervention [kcNFrNC2BIg @ 00:46:46]. Bill Nettles, U.S. Attorney for South Carolina, works the 90 days under seal hard. His office issues CIDs and takes depositions while it decides whether it wants to get in the case [yiUS5Zf9HRI @ 00:19:18]. On the relator side, Mary Ann Hamilton of Miller Law Group says the statutory seal reads 90 days but in practice is never under 120 days. She has watched seals run a year or two, and in one matter about five years [H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:09:43]. The operator consensus is blunt. Budget for a multi-year sealed phase, treat every extension as routine, and package the case so the government can act inside a compressed window that keeps getting tighter.

The second point of agreement is that the relator pool has widened far beyond the disgruntled insider. McGuireWoods' FCA Insider team lists insiders, competitors, and CMS data miners as live relator categories. The team also notes that courts threw out suits brought by a defendant's former counsel [J3hHvouRce8 @ 00:02:59]. Allison Hawthorne of Beasley Allen previews panels on corporations and professional data miners, including the split between 'true corporate relator versus corporate fiction.' Her panel also covers drug manufacturers suing competitors and the relator coalitions formed because these cases 'can be very expensive' [ujkR1nAOen8 @ 00:00:42]. The 2024 FBA panel featuring DOJ Civil Fraud assistant director Ed Crook and Constantine Cannon's Michael Roniker widens the list further. It adds customers, patients, clients, third-party vendors, consultants, and industry experts who mine publicly available data in ways DOJ 'may not have the capability or or means to do' [aZd6GqRekxQ @ 00:03:21]. Hamilton confirms that the insider requirement bends in customs cases brought by competitors [H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:17:52]. Every one of these channels still runs through the same qualifying hurdles: first-to-file, public disclosure, and anonymity, including Doe relators. For an analytics-driven operator, outsider data mining is a recognized relator lane, but it lives or dies on clearing those bars.

Third, practitioners agree that intervention is the lever that moves money, and that neither declination nor dismissal is a merits verdict. McGuireWoods puts intervention at 21 to 24 percent of cases. Over the same period, qui tam filings doubled from the 350-to-400 range in 2008 to 782 last year [J3hHvouRce8 @ 00:09:07]. Hayes insists declinations reflect cost and recoverable dollars rather than merits. He notes that some complaints are 'three pieces of paper' alleging billion-dollar fraud, and that relators have won large judgments after declination [kcNFrNC2BIg @ 00:42:21]. Husch Blackwell's Tanner Cook and Jonathan Porter stress that DOJ dismisses cases for abuse that undermines the purpose of the False Claims Act, not for bad facts or weak pleading. Weak cases are left for courts to resolve at the pleading stage or at summary judgment [XAVzMsuvKNE @ 00:02:08]. The Phillips & Cohen panel anchors the stakes: 85 percent of recoveries come from whistleblower cases and only 15 percent from government-initiated matters [5twGfbHBnJs @ 00:19:33]. The baseline prerequisite follows directly. The relator's package has to be strong enough to win intervention, or the relator and counsel must be resourced enough to survive a declination and litigate the case themselves through discovery.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The unit economics start with the penalty stack. McGuireWoods' FCA Insider team prices each false claim at $11,665 to $22,331 on top of trebled damages, which makes claim count the first input in any exposure model [J3hHvouRce8 @ 00:04:29]. The payout curve then depends on who carries the case. Husch Blackwell's Tanner Cook notes that relators can collect up to one-third of the recovery in non-intervened cases. That pull is strong enough that some interviewees in existing investigations file duplicate suits of their own, which is the conduct targeted by the Granston memo's 'parasitic' dismissal category [XAVzMsuvKNE @ 00:09:49]. In intervened cases, relator counsel Sarah Frazier explains that a share of 20 percent or more requires extraordinary measures, such as wearing a wire for the government [vHZhDg8Ml14 @ 00:12:18]. Blake Percival's USIS case shows the result. The background-investigation dumping fraud against OPM ended in a settlement of about $30 million, and Percival collected 20 percent, about $6 million, within a statutory range of 10 to 30 percent [FopC1sCa2y8 @ 00:56:47]. The working sequence is to count the claims, multiply by the per-claim penalty, treble the damages, and then discount the total for the years the case will spend under seal before any check clears.

Evidence intake is where the craft lives. Leslie Skillin of Getnick & Getnick runs a three-step screen. First, ask whether any document was sent to, from, or copied to an attorney, and whether an attorney was present on a recording. Second, segregate those materials and hire outside ethics counsel to review them. Third, leave crime-fraud determinations to the court on in-camera review [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:05:30]. Hamilton's rule is never to take documents a client would not normally access and to stay targeted. She also tells clients to avoid work email and work machines, and to fall back on detailed notes when the only access runs through company systems [H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:10:36]. The Phillips & Cohen panel says the winning delivery is 'boxed fruit': evidence, a draft subpoena, and an org chart handed to the government [5twGfbHBnJs @ 00:44:29]. Percival's proof was a single flash drive of spreadsheets. It showed that USIS reviewer headcount could not physically process the volume of investigations submitted, and that capacity-versus-throughput analysis exposed the dumping scheme [FopC1sCa2y8 @ 00:36:36]. Taken together, the mechanic is surgical extraction plus a government-ready roadmap, never a bulk folder grab. A clean, narrow package arrives faster and survives the privilege fights that follow.

Settlement is a sequencing game. Mediator Steve Altman, a veteran of more than 40 FCA mediations, settles the scope of the release before any money talk. He tells parties not to offer a lump sum that includes fees, exchanges mediation memos with the other side, and notes that DOJ may allow 60 days to resolve administrative remedies [vHZhDg8Ml14 @ 00:46:04]. King & Spalding's Mike Paulus shows why the fee rule matters. In a $10 million pot carrying $1.5 million in fees, the client might have settled at $8.5 million. He also reports that relator counsel split about 50/50 on negotiating fees alongside the merits [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:50:12]. Kristen Nedwick of the Texas Medicaid Fraud Control Unit warns that multistate deals can require up to 53 separate state agreements. States take up to 60 days to return signed agreements, and states with §1909-compliant statutes pocket an extra 10 percent of the Medicaid share [vHZhDg8Ml14 @ 00:34:31]. DOJ's Sarah McLean adds that cooperation credit is likely to mean about a 1.5x multiplier [vHZhDg8Ml14 @ 00:56:59]. The operator order of operations is release scope, then damages, then fees, then the state paperwork. Mixing those steps is how two-day mediations collapse over whether a number included fees.

callout.title: What the Veterans Do Differently
callout.body: Four moves practitioners on both sides of the bar use to keep a case clean, funded, and alive through the lifecycle.
items: Do not rummage. The CFAA criminalizes unauthorized access, so tell the government where the documents sit and let it subpoena them [ABA Criminal Justice Section — JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:09:12].

Read severance paperwork before signing. Percival's $42,000 severance carried a fine-print waiver of whistleblower rights, and their lawyer's advice was 'don't sign anything' [Whistleblower Heroes — FopC1sCa2y8 @ 00:33:04].
Keep case facts out of AI tools. Hamilton warns AI is not privileged, can be subpoenaed, and gives wrong legal answers, while a Google search is fine [Against The Fraud — H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:26:51].
When asking DOJ to dismiss, fit the request into a Granston memo category, because arguing 'we're right' to DOJ fails [Husch Blackwell — XAVzMsuvKNE @ 00:05:18].

sop_steps.title: Story-and-Goal Intake
sop_steps.action: Open with the whistleblower's story, then pin down their goal and prune facts with no government money attached.
sop_steps.detail: Hamilton starts with 'tell me your story,' then asks 'what's your goal?' Some matters go the employment route instead of qui tam, and facts with no government money attached are reduced to supporting facts [Against The Fraud — H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:06:36].

sop_steps.title: Privilege Segregation Screen
sop_steps.action: Flag every attorney-touched document or recording, segregate it, and route it to outside ethics counsel.
sop_steps.detail: Skillin segregates materials sent to, from, or copied to an attorney and hires outside ethics counsel to review them. Wiseman warns that privileged productions delay DOJ, force taint review, and can disqualify the assigned attorneys [ABA Criminal Justice Section — JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:06:51].

sop_steps.title: Build the Boxed-Fruit Package
sop_steps.action: Deliver evidence, a draft subpoena, and an org chart so the government can move inside the seal window.
sop_steps.detail: The Phillips & Cohen panel tells relators to bring the government 'boxed fruit': evidence, a draft subpoena, and an org chart [Phillips & Cohen LLP — 5twGfbHBnJs @ 00:44:29].

sop_steps.title: Partner Through the Seal
sop_steps.action: Work alongside the U.S. Attorney's office during the sealed investigation rather than waiting on the sidelines.
sop_steps.detail: Nettles rejects the 'we'll call you when it's over' model. Relators' counsel share the burden as partners, and his office advocates for a larger relator share in return [Emory School of Law — yiUS5Zf9HRI @ 00:26:21].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The seal clock is the first fault line, and practitioners read it differently depending on which side of the docket they sit. Bill Nettles, U.S. Attorney for South Carolina, treats the seal as a working window: "we have 90 days under seal to decide whether we want to get in the case or not," and inside that window the office issues CIDs and takes depositions [yiUS5Zf9HRI @ 00:19:18]. Mary Ann Hamilton of Miller Law Group calls the statutory number a fiction: the seal is never under 120 days, has run a year or two, and in one matter ran about five years [H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:09:43]. Rich Hayes, EDNY Civil Deputy Chief, attacks the clock from inside government, calling 60 days "not a lot of time" to figure out whether a multi-billion dollar fraud occurred [kcNFrNC2BIg @ 00:46:46]. Hayes adds that courts are allowing less time to decide intervention, which squeezes the government further. Amanda Roach of USAO-Colorado frames the seal as at least 60 days serving three purposes, with partial lifts available and a Fourth Circuit rule that a relator may discuss the allegations but not the action [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:40:25]. Budget for Hamilton's reality, not the statute's headline number.

The second split is over what DOJ dismissals and declinations actually signal. Jonathan Porter and Tanner Cook of Husch Blackwell report DOJ dismissals jumping from around six a year to around 25, yet insist "DOJ isn't looking to dismiss weak cases"; dismissal targets abuse that undermines the statute, and weak cases are left for pleading or summary judgment [XAVzMsuvKNE @ 00:22:44]. The McGuireWoods team hears a different story on the ground: DOJ attorneys say the Granston memo "didn't change anything," but in practice DOJ has told relators' counsel to dismiss [J3hHvouRce8 @ 00:42:18]. Rich Hayes rejects reading declination as a merits verdict at all: declinations reflect cost and recoverable dollars, some complaints are "three pieces of paper" alleging billion-dollar fraud, and relators have won large judgments after the government walked away [kcNFrNC2BIg @ 00:42:21]. The Phillips & Cohen panel describes a far harsher funnel, about 700 cases filed a year with the government intervening in about 15, well below the 21 to 24 percent intervention rate McGuireWoods reports [5twGfbHBnJs @ 00:44:44]. Porter and Cook add a tactical warning for defendants who want DOJ to kill a case: arguing "we're right" fails, and the request has to fit one of the seven Granston categories.

Fee handling inside global settlements splits the bar almost down the middle. Mike Paulus of King & Spalding reports relator counsel split about 50/50 on negotiating fees alongside the merits, and runs the math: a $10M pot with $1.5M in fees means the client might have settled at $8.5M [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:50:12]. Leslie Skillin of Getnick & Getnick, on the relator side, pushes back that this is not an issue in intervened cases [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:54:51]. Mediator Steve Altman, with more than 40 FCA mediations on the books, takes a hard line the other way: do not offer a lump sum that includes fees, and settle the scope of the release before agreeing on money [vHZhDg8Ml14 @ 00:47:11]. Paulus floats the opposite fix, saying that putting fees into the shared pot "might" resolve the conflict, while DOJ's David Wiseman recalls a two-day mediation that ended in a dispute over whether the number included fees [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:59:21]. Paulus ties the conflict to Rules 1.2, 1.4, 1.5, 1.7 informed written consent, and 1.8, plus written allocation among multiple relators, with the panel stressing that any offer from opposing counsel must be promptly relayed to the client. Pick a lane before mediation, not during it.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive self-inflicted wound is the evidence grab. In Cafasso, the relator took 11 GB, the NDA counterclaim was upheld, and $300,000 in fees was awarded; the account of how it happened is damning on its own: "i just grabbed the whole folder um she didn't read the files she just read the file names" [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:11:12]. Mike Paulus confirms defense clients pursue counterclaims for improper access, and the panel flags that "rummaging" is a factor and that the CFAA criminalizes unauthorized access, so the better play is telling the government where documents sit so it can subpoena them [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:09:12]. Privilege is the second trap: David Wiseman warns that privileged productions delay DOJ, force taint review, and can disqualify the attorneys assigned [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:07:36]. Mary Ann Hamilton draws the same line from the relator side: never take documents you would not normally access, be targeted, avoid work email and work machines, and never feed case data to AI because it is not privileged, can be subpoenaed, and gives wrong legal answers [H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:10:52]. Hamilton's verdict on overreach: it "can very quickly undermine the legitimacy of a case and it can get you in trouble all on its own."

Seal breaches and settlement paperwork are where money leaks after the case is already won. The ABA panel stresses that "it's not an automatic dismissal if the relator breaches the seal," but the bill still comes due: in Bibi v. Wells Fargo, DOJ recommended $2.7M, the share above the 25 percent minimum, and the court ordered $1.6M [JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:48:18]. Defendants hit the seal problem too; Mike Paulus says insurers create a catch-22, so Paulus seeks an extra partial lift. Sarah Frazier warns that a common reason for a government veto is too much of the settlement allocated to the retaliation claim, and the panel says to tell DOJ about any retaliation claim in advance [vHZhDg8Ml14 @ 00:06:14]. Exit paperwork is the employee-side trap: the McGuireWoods team notes FCA claims cannot be released, but the recovery can, meaning a departing employee who signs can lose the right to share in any recovery [J3hHvouRce8 @ 00:55:28]. Blake Percival lived that trap: severance was $42,000 with a fine-print waiver of whistleblower rights, and their lawyer's advice was "don't sign anything" [FopC1sCa2y8 @ 00:31:22]. Refusing that $42,000 kept the path open to the roughly $6M, 20 percent share Percival later received.

The economics check is time, and every practitioner who has lived a case reports it running longer than planned. Blake Percival filed a sealed qui tam on July 1, 2011 through Beasley Allen after being fired in May 2011, then sat through 60-to-90-day continuances for years; a June 2013 hardship settlement attempt was derailed by the Snowden hearings, and DOJ intervened only on October 30, 2013 [FopC1sCa2y8 @ 00:38:39]. The firing alone cost six figures in pay, a $20K bonus, an SUV and an Amex. The settlement came to about $30M, with Percival taking 20 percent, about $6M, against fraud that ran across 665,000 investigations and a Wall Street Journal estimate of seven point six billion dollars if fully prosecuted, and Percival reports being blackballed in the industry afterward [FopC1sCa2y8 @ 00:56:47]. On the litigation side, a DC Circuit case ran 12 years, with three years of discovery and a million documents, before dismissal at summary judgment [kcNFrNC2BIg @ 00:06:14]. The McGuireWoods team tracks Ruckh, where a $340M verdict was vacated before $85M was reinstated in June 2020 [J3hHvouRce8 @ 00:24:35]. The defendants' lever there was materiality: they "moved for judgment as a matter of law arguing that none of their uh purported misstatements were material."

callout.title: Stop Before You Copy, Sign, Breach or Settle
callout.body: Every item below is a loss practitioners watched happen: fee awards against relators, forfeited shares, vetoed deals and waived recoveries. Clear all four before moving to the next lifecycle stage.
items: Before taking any document, confirm it is one you normally access and that it targets the fraud; the Cafasso 11 GB folder grab ended in a $300,000 fee award [ABA Criminal Justice Section — JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:11:12].

Ask whether any document or recording involved an attorney, segregate those materials, and route them to outside ethics counsel before DOJ sees them [ABA Criminal Justice Section — JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:06:51].
Do not sign severance or exit paperwork that waives whistleblower rights; Percival turned down $42,000 on the advice 'don't sign anything' [Whistleblower Heroes — FopC1sCa2y8 @ 00:33:04].
Under seal, defendants consult the AUSA before disclosing to the SEC, insurers or buyers, and seek a partial lift rather than risk a breach [ABA Criminal Justice Section — JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:40:25].

chapters.pull_quote: "A false claims act claim is a lie attached to a dollar." — Against The Fraud (H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:25:38)
action_checklist: Open intake with 'tell me your story,' then ask 'what's your goal?' and route matters with no government money to the employment track [Against The Fraud — H0ay64A0XXA @ 00:06:36].
Bring the government 'boxed fruit': the evidence, a draft subpoena and an org chart, so investigators can move inside the seal window [Phillips & Cohen LLP — 5twGfbHBnJs @ 00:44:29].

Ask whether any document was sent to, from or copied to an attorney, or whether an attorney was on a recording, and segregate those items for outside ethics counsel [ABA Criminal Justice Section — JN4iipJiHZM @ 00:05:30].

On the defense side, answer a CID with open DOJ communication, document preservation and custodial interviews, because slow-rolling invites a search warrant or unsealing [McGuireWoods LLP — J3hHvouRce8 @ 00:47:29].
In mediation, settle the scope of the release before agreeing on money, and exchange mediation memos with the other side [ABA Criminal Justice Section — vHZhDg8Ml14 @ 00:46:04].
Coordinate with co-relators early, since DOJ wants cooperation and may give its opinion on who provided the first information [The Employment Law Group, P.C. — ukz2VRmDQIs @ 00:04:41].

chapters.question_prompt: How is DOJ using data analytics and shifting enforcement priorities to find FCA fraud, and where is that enforcement headed?
chapters.title: Data-Mined Enforcement: How DOJ Algorithms and Priorities Drive FCA Cases
chapters.subtitle: Claims-data mining and statistical sampling, DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division and early seizures, the DOJ–HHS FCA task force and national healthcare fraud takedown, Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment cases, COVID-relief fraud, and annual FCA enforcement trend reviews
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Foley & Lardner, Seyfarth Shaw, Epstein Becker Green, Reed Smith and Analysis Group converge on one picture: DOJ is centralizing FCA enforcement, healthcare dominates the money, and data miners now drive a large slice of the docket. FY2025 recoveries topped $6.8B, with $5.7B from healthcare, roughly 1,300 qui tams filed, and data miners behind more than 45% of qui tams since FY2024. The street mechanics are concrete: the FOCUS initiative demands correlations tethered to falsity and scienter, Rule 9(b) is the first motion-to-dismiss weapon against algorithmic complaints, CID signatures reveal case value, and a civil self-disclosure pilot prices repayment at 1.25-1.6x. Disagreement centers on filing counts, cyber recovery totals, relator share ranges, and whether DOJ will actually use its dismissal power against weak declined cases.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus: Central Command, Healthcare Money and the Rise of Data Miners
paragraphs: Enforcement is being pulled toward Main Justice and pointed at healthcare. Erica Sibley Bondson and Leah Brownlee Taylor of Epstein Becker Green walk through the new National Fraud Enforcement Division, which absorbed the criminal Tax section, the Health Care Fraud Unit and MGCF, with civil components possibly added later; Leah expects top-down, centralized, hands-on control from Main Justice rather than scattered U.S. Attorney discretion [rxUll524o5w @ 00:03:00]. Jennifer Seraphin of Seyfarth Shaw confirms that Directive 26-12 makes healthcare the top priority, backed by strike forces in New England and on the West Coast and a dedicated fraud division inside the DC U.S. Attorney's Office [QLVKZRh_ArE @ 00:16:20]. Jonathan Porter of Husch Blackwell, a DOJ alum, reports staff being moved off antitrust and securities work and onto healthcare files, and the episode closes with the blunt line that healthcare enforcement is coming [FO7NfNf-r0k @ 00:00:30]. The money backs the staffing: the Foley & Lardner panel says 84% of the dollars the government recovered last fiscal year came from healthcare, inside a record-breaking $6.8B year [J1-aE0W1Eu8 @ 00:09:37]. For an operator, the baseline assumption is simple: healthcare claims sit at the center of the target map, and the decisions about them increasingly come from a central command that sets targets before local offices ever touch a file.

Every serious panel agrees the docket is being fed by data, not just insiders. Analysis Group's panel reports that almost all FCA cases historically came from insider whistleblowers, then DOJ officials from 2019 through 2022 started saying they were using big data to find payment anomalies, with an ultrasound statistical-outlier case and four PEMF electro-acupuncture cases cited as proof [y9nEr_YUXBY @ 00:08:09]. Epstein Becker Green puts a number on the relator side: data miners have filed more than 45% of qui tams since FY2024, and a new whistleblower program pays $10-30,000 per tip [rxUll524o5w @ 00:16:24]. Tom Sutis and David Bender of Reed Smith describe an upsurge of non-insider whistleblowers using public data and AI tools, driven by DOJ priority, newly public data and the relator's share of the recovery, with healthcare as the main hunting ground [mNX2NY20ks0 @ 00:03:44]. Relator counsel Shawna Itri of Seeger Weiss traces the fuel back to CMS releasing claims data in 2011, and lists data-driven settlements of $280M and $98M plus Integra settlements of $61M and $188M [SKjmFHwe2Rk @ 00:33:33]. The consensus mechanic: public claims data plus AI tools plus a 15-30% relator share turns outsiders into relators who never worked a day inside the target company.

The same practitioners agree on the ceiling: data flags anomalies, but it does not prove fraud. The Reed Smith pair put it flatly, correlation does not equate to causation, and the scienter or knowing element is what separates an overpayment from fraud [mNX2NY20ks0 @ 00:11:53]. Analysis Group's panel adds that data cannot prove scienter under the FCA knowingly standard, let alone the higher anti-kickback intent standard, and that outputs are vulnerable to the data-generating process, such as how clinicians order tests [y9nEr_YUXBY @ 00:23:24]. The proof is the Integra Med Analytics line: Epstein Becker Green notes the Fifth Circuit dismissed the Baylor Scott & White suit in 2020 because obvious alternative explanations existed, and Analysis Group adds the Ninth Circuit did the same to the Providence suit, even though DOJ did intervene in an Integra nursing-home RUGs case [rxUll524o5w @ 00:18:26]. On the defense side, Josh Drew holds that traditional compliance still works, with an effective reporting line, internal investigations and remediation at the top of the list, because whistleblowers usually raise concerns internally first [zF0bNkCTI_Q @ 00:10:23]. The baseline prerequisite for anyone mining claims or defending against miners is identical: a statistical outlier must be married to a falsity theory and hard evidence of knowledge.

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The newest rulebook for algorithmic cases is DOJ's FOCUS initiative, announced at the end of April 2026, short for fraud oversight through careful use of statistics, which sets guardrails on FCA data mining [mNX2NY20ks0 @ 00:03:06]. The Reed Smith team explains why it exists: reduced DOJ staff are facing record 2026 filings, so FOCUS is meant to winnow the pile, and what DOJ will accept is a reliable correlation tethered to legal analysis of falsity and scienter rather than a raw statistical spike [mNX2NY20ks0 @ 00:16:39]. Speed is built into the review: Jennifer Seraphin reports the Shumate memo sets a 60-day seal review with a 120-day maximum, and describes two intake tracks, vetted data miners on one side and interagency or OIG referrals on the other [QLVKZRh_ArE @ 00:23:51]. On the pleading battlefield, Rule 9(b) heightened particularity is the first motion-to-dismiss defense against data-built complaints, a higher bar than an ordinary nonfraud civil case, and the AHLA panel points to Hanagan v. Amazon in the Second Circuit as requiring scienter facts under Rule 9(b), offsetting the subjective-knowledge standard of SuperValu that otherwise makes cases harder to kill early [U_YfcwE9PJk @ 00:20:16]. The street read: a miner who files a bare outlier chart is feeding a dismissal motion.

The modeling playbook comes from Analysis Group's panel. Builders choose between supervised machine learning trained on known fraud and unsupervised outlier and association-rule detection, while deep learning and tree ensembles are flagged as black boxes that raise bias concerns [y9nEr_YUXBY @ 00:15:28]. Models are screening tools followed by deeper human review; the panel urges CRISP-DM as the workflow, treating model flags like whistleblower complaints, and balancing false positives against false negatives with an F1 score [y9nEr_YUXBY @ 00:44:42]. The panel's sharpest line is to start with simple things first and not get cute with machine learning, which tracks with how Integra Med Analytics built its cases on simple statistics claiming 1 in 100,000 odds [y9nEr_YUXBY @ 00:27:54]. AI now runs on both sides of the caption: Sutis and Bender report relators using AI to draft complaints, defendants using AI to dig up counterexamples showing a pattern of compliance, and some courts requiring counsel to certify AI use [mNX2NY20ks0 @ 00:20:36]. The compliance flip is the same toolkit pointed inward: pharma should mine call patterns, HCP payments and prescriptions for outliers, and DOJ in the Walmart opioid matter pointed at the company's own wealth of dispensing information.

The response numbers are where operators make or lose money. Michael Podberesky of McGuireWoods, ex-DOJ Civil Fraud, reads the signature first: a local U.S. Attorney signals a matter under $10M, while the Civil Fraud Director in Washington signals $10M or more, and the statutory clock runs 20 days for documents and as little as 7 days for oral testimony [JXEl43HAAuo @ 00:09:41]. Tori Young of Seyfarth Shaw prices the exit: the civil self-disclosure pilot runs to April 22, 2027 with repayment at 1.25-1.6x and no factual admissions, CIA, CMPs or revocations, against typical settlements near 2x, with the AKS repayment base set at remuneration rather than claims paid [QLVKZRh_ArE @ 00:30:43]. On the bounty side, relators take 15-30% plus a new tipster track of $10-30,000, while Evan Gotlab of DarrowEverett puts the share upwards of 35% and walks a $20M claim to roughly $6-7M before attorneys take about a third; Gotlab adds that once DOJ is involved, settlements come within 6 months, which compresses the whole fight [5LsJY2Ss1SI @ 00:09:30]. Penalty math is the multiplier that makes mining pay: per-claim penalties stack across thousands or millions of claims, and as Reed Smith puts it, a lot of claims means a lot of penalty [mNX2NY20ks0 @ 00:09:35].
