chapters.question_prompt: Beyond healthcare and defense, where else are FCA and federal-funds whistleblower cases being brought—customs, relief loans, grants, financial fraud, and state FCAs?
chapters.title: Beyond Healthcare: Customs Evasion, Relief Loans, Grants, and State FCAs
chapters.subtitle: Tariff and antidumping evasion via country-of-origin and undervaluation schemes, importer risk, PPP and disaster-loan fraud, research-grant exposure, financial-fraud qui tams, the $25M federal-funds reward program, rising state FCA enforcement, recovery statistics, and case studies
chapters.executive_summary: Customs-fraud qui tam practitioners agree the False Claims Act squarely reaches tariff evasion, and that the attack surface is CBP Form 7501: origin, HTS code, description, and declared value. Tycko & Zavareei's Jon Tycko maps the schemes: undervaluation via dual invoicing, misclassification, transshipment, sham substantial transformation, omitted assists, and de minimis structuring. These run against Section 301 tariffs of 25% and AD/CVD orders reaching hundreds of percent, with only 1-2% of containers inspected. The street math: $2M evaded across 25 shipments becomes roughly $6.5M in liability, relators collect 15-30% (about 17-18% typical), seals average 18 months, and wins take 2.5-3 years. Beyond customs, PPP affiliate concealment, grant charging, and state FCAs paying up to 50% widen the field. Disagreement runs on scienter, intervention odds, and whether state policy enforcement belongs under the FCA.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The customs bar agrees on one thing first: the False Claims Act covers tariff evasion, full stop. John Tio, who has run roughly 15 customs cases since 2012, puts it flatly that "there's no question that the false claims act covers Customs fraud" [MTKHmo8s-kc @ 00:27:22]. Jon Tycko explains the hook: customs cases run on the reverse false claims provision, which needs only a false record and knowing falsity, and importers cannot keep their "head in the sand" [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:04:06]. The false record almost always sits on CBP Form 7501, where four fields carry the lie: country of origin, product description, HTS code, and quantity or value. Shipping Solutions anchors the stakes with a $26 million penalty upheld on appeal against an importer that labeled Chinese goods as Taiwanese to dodge antidumping duties [EIHwzCe4zZM @ 00:00:06]. Brown, LLC reduces the field to two dominant plays: stripping certain basis costs out of dutiable value and falsifying country of origin, typically by drop-shipping China-tariffed goods, roughly 25% exposure, through a third country [XXtgvEhkvo4 @ 00:00:54]. Tax liability itself is carved out of the federal FCA and routes to IRS or anti-money-laundering programs, so the customs relator works duties, not income tax. Every scheme the practitioners describe ultimately resolves to a provably false line on an entry form.

Second point of consensus: the government cannot see this fraud without insiders, and tariff spikes are manufacturing more of it. Tio cites statistics that only 1% or maybe 2% of all containers get inspected, and warns that origin fraud is "very hard to detect without whistleblowers" because CBP has little visibility into supply chains [MTKHmo8s-kc @ 00:21:23]. Steve Teller describes the incentive engine: sudden tariff hikes catch importers who picked price points under the old rates, and that "really increases the incentives for them to be dishonest" [QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:00:48]. Jason T. Brown predicted more customs cases built on circumvention of China tariffs and said the government wants to "make an example" of drop-ship schemes dressed up with a superficial or cosmetic change [5fDm1yVZ4cM @ 00:00:41]. Tycko says the relator pool is wide open: individuals or entities, insiders or outsiders, competitors, even trade associations, and foreign relators are allowed [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:16:41]. Tio adds that higher tariffs hand cheaters a competitive edge, and names competitors, industry insiders, and employees as the relators who surface it. The operator read is simple: the people closest to sourcing, pricing, and logistics hold the evidence CBP lacks, and every new tariff layer widens the gap between honest and cheating importers.

The consensus carries past the docks into relief loans, grants, and state statutes. Brown says viable PPP cases center on borrowers that concealed affiliates to slip under the 500-employee or $10 million cap [5fDm1yVZ4cM @ 00:03:09]. Cheryl Burch of USC's Institute for Creative Technologies tells research administrators they are exposed when they process a grant expense they know does not benefit the project or submit a proposal with inaccurate statements, because the Act reaches "a false statement that leads to a false claim" [oh1aiSdEJHY @ 00:00:53]. Rebecca Ferdick of Husch Blackwell flags that state FCAs vary widely: California pays relators up to 50% in non-intervened cases against 25-30% federally, some states cover claims to political subdivisions, and some reach tax claims [_n3NJXxKz_8 @ 00:03:13]. Across all of it, the knowledge standard is the shared baseline. Shipping Solutions defines "knowingly" to include actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard, and notes the whistleblower takes a share of the recovery [EIHwzCe4zZM @ 00:01:15]. Minnesota's statute, about 15 years old and not limited to Medicaid, carries roughly $27,000 per claim, and its AG already chased false COVID rental-assistance claims. For an operator, that means customs, PPP, grants, and state money all run through the same knowing-falsity filter.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The unit economics are concrete. Tycko walks a model case: $2 million in evaded duty across 25 shipments converts to roughly $6.5 million in liability once treble damages and per-shipment penalties stack [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:25:04]. Relator share runs 15-25% when the government intervenes and 25-30% when it declines; he pegs 15% of $6.5 million at "$925,000," though the arithmetic lands near $975,000, and says awards average "about 18%" [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:29:15]. Teller's field number is tighter: about 17% is typical, the realistic band is 15-25%, and anything above 20% is hard to get; one cable-company recovery of $40 million paid the relator 16%, stated as $6.5 million and described as "really life-changing money" [QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:12:30]. On the relief-loan side, PilieroMazza's Matt Feinberg prices penalties at $11,665 to $23,331 per claim and shows a $5 million contract turning into $15 million in treble damages [eIBPl3LNUXQ @ 00:09:59]. Feinberg also reports that 25-40% of FCA cases originate with the government itself. Fees shift to the defendant, and most relator counsel work on contingency, so the relator fronts no hourly bill. Tycko's customs scoreboard for 2011 to 2023: 43 settlements, 42 of them relator-driven, more than $220 million recovered, and more than $20 million paid out in rewards.

Execution hinges on surviving procedure. Tycko's public disclosure trap is the first filter: raw, unanalyzed data is generally not treated as a public disclosure, which matters for anyone building a case from import data [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:17:20]. Filing is "a secret filing" under seal; the statute says 60 days, but the seal averages about 18 months, and breaking it risks losing the reward or getting the case dismissed [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:20:33]. During that window the government can intervene, decline, or dismiss over the relator's objection, and successful cases take 2.5 to 3 years or more. Brown warns that first-to-file rules can leave later filers with nothing, and that relator-versus-relator disputes get "ugly" and are often settled quietly [5fDm1yVZ4cM @ 00:09:45]. Teller's pre-filing sequence for insiders: research the issue first, raise it with your boss if the goal is to fix it, and call FCA counsel if the boss turns defensive; calling an employment lawyer early is "a great idea," and complaints should be documented strategically, from an informal "crayon" note to a formal HR escalation [QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:14:41]. Tycko counts only about 500 specialist lawyers nationwide in this space, and names the importer of record, overseas suppliers, downstream retailers, and owners as potential defendants.

Operators also price the alternative channels. Tycko says CBP's e-Allegations route, which needs Form 4623, and EAPA claims, limited to AD/CVD and directly affected parties, cap rewards at $250,000 and operate as a CBP "black box" compared with a qui tam [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:34:59]. On the state side, Husch Blackwell's Todd G. walks a DC tax FCA where a Bitcoin investor allegedly evaded about $25 million through false residency claims, including false W-2 addresses, and the matter settled for $40 million, then adds New York's 2021 Fanatics matter, more than $1.5 million over undercollected sales tax; the firm also cites a Massachusetts runway case that settled for $3 million with nearly $1.5 million more recovered federally [_n3NJXxKz_8 @ 00:14:04]. For financial fraud, Tycko & Zavareei lists at least five avenues: the FCA, SEC, CFTC, DOJ banking, and Treasury/BSA, each paying a percentage of actual recovery under its own procedures, with few reports reaching an award, so submissions must be compelling [azRmbEExKOw @ 00:00:23]. The National Desk reports a new $25 million whistleblower program pitched with a "1% commission" and $260 billion in uncovered fraud, but "just reporting suspected fraud won't automatically get you a check": payment requires a conviction or significant enforcement action [yWSbhn3NK9w @ 00:01:55].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is how much intent a case needs. K2 GRC sells the FCA as a near strict-liability hammer: treble damages plus an inflation-linked per-claim penalty that, in their telling, applies "even if it was an accident" and even to information submitted "unknowingly" [BgDdBSZpEjc @ 00:01:00]. The customs specialists run a tighter standard. Shipping Solutions defines "knowingly" as actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard [EIHwzCe4zZM @ 00:01:15]. Jon Tycko of Tycko & Zavareei builds customs cases on the reverse false claims provision with two required elements, a false record and knowing falsity, and stresses that importers cannot put their "head in the sand" [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:05:42]. Steve Teller draws the line that matters inside tariff-classification work: misstating what an item actually is counts as fraud, while choosing between two plausible HTS categories sits closer to a regulatory question [QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:02:46]. For a data-mining relator the playbook difference is real. K2 GRC's framing would treat every coding error as a payday, but the litigators who actually file customs cases want evidence of deliberate conduct, reckless disregard, or a willful blind spot. A file built on a defensible judgment call between two codes is the weakest pitch an operator can bring to relator counsel.

Payout expectations diverge by channel and by lawyer. Tycko quotes the federal bands as 15 to 25 percent when the government intervenes and 25 to 30 percent when it declines [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:26:11]. Teller is more guarded about the top of the range: roughly 17 percent is typical, the band runs 15 to 25, and getting above 20 percent is hard [QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:12:30]. Rebecca Ferdick of Husch Blackwell points to the state-level outlier, California, which pays relators up to 50 percent in non-intervened cases against 25 to 30 percent federally [_n3NJXxKz_8 @ 00:03:13]. The administrative routes sit at the other end of the spectrum. Tycko describes CBP's e-Allegations and EAPA routes as a "black box" that caps rewards at $250,000, with EAPA confined to AD/CVD and directly affected parties [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:34:59]. That cap is the pivot for route selection. A relator sitting on a multi-million-dollar evasion pattern leaves most of the upside on the table by going administrative, while the qui tam route keeps the reward tied to treble damages and per-claim penalties. The trade is a capped, opaque administrative payout against a sealed, multi-year fight, with fee-shifting and contingency counsel absorbing the cost.

Forum, constitutionality, and tax coverage are all live fights. John Tio, appearing on Fraud in America, flags the Island Industries ruling in the Ninth Circuit, where the court may require customs FCA claims to be filed in the Court of International Trade, yet Tio still files Ninth Circuit cases [MTKHmo8s-kc @ 00:26:42]. Robert Salo of Akin Gump, a former DOJ Civil Fraud lawyer on the American Health Law Association panel, reports that the "zaurov" decision held the qui tam provisions violate the Appointments Clause, and that defendants now raise the argument routinely and move to quash CIDs [xaaGMrYhE60 @ 00:12:25]. Tax is the third split. Brown, LLC tells customs whistleblowers that tax liability is carved out of the FCA and routes to the IRS or anti-money-laundering programs instead [XXtgvEhkvo4 @ 00:00:22]. Husch Blackwell's Todd G. sees the state side moving the opposite way, citing a DC Bitcoin investor who allegedly dodged about $25 million in tax through false residency claims in a case that settled for $40 million, and arguing it "just makes too much sense" for governments to chase tax evasion through FCA mechanisms [_n3NJXxKz_8 @ 00:16:36]. Read them as filters: federal customs files run through qui tam, state tax files need a statute that reaches tax, and Appointments Clause motions add delay.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Procedure kills more relator files than weak facts. Tycko warns the seal runs 60 days by statute but averages about 18 months, and breaking it risks losing the reward or getting the case dismissed [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:20:33]. The public disclosure bar is the next tripwire, though Tycko notes raw, unanalyzed data is generally not treated as a public disclosure, which is exactly what keeps a data-mined import case alive when the relator supplies the analysis [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:17:20]. Jason T. Brown of Brown, LLC flags the race condition: first-to-file rules can leave later filers with nothing, and the resulting disputes are "ugly" and often settled quietly [5fDm1yVZ4cM @ 00:09:45]. Tycko & Zavareei's financial-fraud briefing adds the volume problem: few reports lead to awards, so the submission has to be compelling [azRmbEExKOw @ 00:01:57]. Put together, the operating rule is speed plus silence plus analysis. File before a competitor or a co-worker beats you to the courthouse, say nothing outside counsel while the seal holds, and hand the government a worked theory instead of a pile of shipping records. A relator who leaks, waits, or dumps unprocessed data gives defendants three separate exits before the merits are ever reached.

The employee-relator path carries personal risk that the lawyers describe from live cases. Teller recounts an extruded-aluminum AD/CVD matter where a bike-rack maker owed about $1 million but disclosed only about $400,000; the client objected, was let go, and the company ended up paying about $3.4 million [QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:05:33]. Teller's fix is sequencing: research the issue, raise it with the boss if the goal is to fix it, and call an employment lawyer early rather than after the termination letter [QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:14:41]. Evidence quality is the other trap. Matt Feinberg of PilieroMazza, arguing from the defense side, points to a case built on secondhand happy-hour gossip that was dismissed [eIBPl3LNUXQ @ 00:58:01]. Inside universities, Cheryl Burch of USC's Institute for Creative Technologies lays out the slower internal path for research administrators: get an email from the researcher justifying the charge, and if it still doesn't make sense, share it with the departmental or central campus representative [oh1aiSdEJHY @ 00:02:00]. The common thread is documentation before confrontation. A relator who escalates without paper, or who relies on what colleagues repeated at the bar, hands the defense an easy dismissal and exposes their own job with nothing to show for it.

Run the arithmetic yourself before pitching counsel or a client, because even the practitioners' own figures drift. Tycko prices a 15 percent share of an example $6.5 million liability at "$925,000" [A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:26:11]; 15 percent of $6.5 million is about $975,000. Teller describes a $40 million cable-company recovery paying 16 percent, stated as $6.5 million, and calls it "really life-changing money" [QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:13:09]; 16 percent of $40 million is $6.4 million. Feinberg's defense math shows the downside a defendant prices in: penalties of $11,665 to $23,331 per claim on top of treble damages [eIBPl3LNUXQ @ 00:09:59]. Michael Sanchez of Compliance Mitigation anchors the realistic outcome with WorkRite's GSA MAS pricing case, which settled for $7.1 million and paid the relator $1.27 million [3kDd1dqYkWY @ 00:09:33]. That works out to roughly 18 percent, landing right on Tycko's historical customs average. Model payouts at 15 to 18 percent of the actual settlement, not of the theoretical treble number, and assume the check arrives years after filing, not months. Anything built on the 25 to 30 percent declined-case band or California's 50 percent ceiling is upside, not the base case.

callout.title: Four checks before a relator file leaves the building
callout.body: Every item below traces to a loss, dismissal, or reversal the practitioners reported. Clear all four before filing or escalating.
items: Seal discipline: no co-worker, competitor, or press contact while the seal holds, which averages about 18 months against a 60-day statutory clock [Tycko & Zavareei LLP — A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:20:33].
Firsthand evidence only: a case resting on secondhand happy-hour gossip was dismissed [PilieroMazza PLLC — eIBPl3LNUXQ @ 00:58:01].

Employment counsel before internal escalation: call an employment lawyer early, because Teller's AD/CVD client who objected to an underpaid disclosure was let go [Stephen Teller - Teller Law — QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:14:41].
Collectability check: D&O insurance often excludes treble damages, so the defendant's policy may not fund the treble portion of a recovery [PilieroMazza PLLC — eIBPl3LNUXQ @ 00:41:04].

chapters.pull_quote: "This is very hard to detect without whistleblowers because the government otherwise doesn't really have a lot of visibility into these supply chains right now." — Fraud in America (MTKHmo8s-kc @ 00:18:59).
action_checklist: Pull the four fraud fields on CBP Form 7501 for each target importer: origin, description, HTS code, and quantity/value [Tycko & Zavareei LLP — A2nRu5da_9k @ 00:06:19].

Screen for dual invoicing and undervaluation, the scheme in a majority of customs cases, where importers tell CBP products are worth less than they really are [Fraud in America — MTKHmo8s-kc @ 00:13:05].
Test every substantial-transformation origin claim against CBP's public letter rulings and flag assembly-country origin claims built on foreign components [Fraud in America — MTKHmo8s-kc @ 00:17:52].
For PPP files, hunt concealed affiliates that push the borrower past the 500-employee or $10 million cap [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 5fDm1yVZ4cM @ 00:03:09].

On federal grants, get the researcher's email justifying the charge, including the allocation method for split expenses, and escalate if it still doesn't make sense [NCURA1959 — oh1aiSdEJHY @ 00:01:45].
Document complaints strategically, from an informal crayon note up to an HR escalation, and call FCA counsel if the boss turns defensive [Stephen Teller - Teller Law — QNzd1e6e8UE @ 00:16:26].

chapters.question_prompt: How does the SEC whistleblower program work, what earns an award, and why are so many claims denied?
chapters.title: The SEC Whistleblower Program: Tips, Awards, and Denials
chapters.subtitle: Dodd-Frank origins, original information and award thresholds, types of securities fraud worth reporting, anonymous filing through counsel, the 31 back-to-back denials, the record $279M bounty, program reform proposals, and corporate implications of the rules
chapters.executive_summary: SEC whistleblower practitioners agree on the core gate: voluntarily hand over original information that drives sanctions above $1 million and collect 10 to 30 percent. They also agree insiders need counsel and an SEC-first route: anonymity requires an attorney, Digital Realty strips Dodd-Frank retaliation protection from anyone who reports only internally, and internal hotlines can expose the insider first. The mechanics run on Form TCR, a 120-day window after internal or other-agency reports, heavy ongoing assistance, and a self-policed claim after the notice of covered action posts. The funnel is brutal: 68 awards from over 18,000 fiscal 2023 tips, then 31 straight denials. Practitioners split on internal reporting, which earns a plus factor under the award rules per Andrew Feller, while Brown, LLC warns compliance lines get insiders fired.

key_metrics.context: Record-breaking award paid to a still-anonymous insider who exposed malfeasance inside a regulated financial company.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who walks through eligibility lands on the same four-part gate. Wiley Rein's white-collar partner, a former SEC enforcement attorney and federal prosecutor, frames it as voluntarily handing over original information about a securities violation that has occurred, is ongoing, or is about to occur, which then drives a successful action with monetary sanctions above $1 million, paying 10 to 30 percent of what the SEC collects; and 'voluntarily' dies the moment any regulator, Congress included, has already asked you or your lawyer for the information [lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:02:09]. Parnham and Associates runs the floor math: at the $1 million threshold the 10 percent minimum still pencils out to a $100,000 check, and SEC fines on publicly traded companies regularly run into the tens of millions and higher [8tuRViP_j4Y @ 00:03:37]. 'Original' means independent knowledge or independent analysis the SEC does not already hold. Chris Ehrman, director of the CFTC whistleblower office, says the analysis route is where outside market experts earn their seat, walking regulators through trading patterns like spoofing that agency surveillance misses because the industry always out-innovates the government [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 00:28:00]. Silver Law Group confirms eligibility reaches current employees, investment-scheme victims, and outside analysts who volunteer new information [AoceOfN67y8 @ 00:00:48].

The loudest consensus is that going it alone is a losing play. Jason T. Brown, a former FBI special agent who runs Brown, LLC, says filing through the TCR portal yourself is strongly discouraged, because only a filing through an SEC whistleblower lawyer lets you stay anonymous from start to finish, and the SEC acts on very few of the thousands of tips it gets, so you get exactly one bite of the apple [b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:03:15]. Parnham and Associates states the anonymity rule flatly: if you report anonymously and still want to be eligible for a monetary award, the tip has to come through your attorney [8tuRViP_j4Y @ 00:04:16]. Andrew Feller, who spent 15 years at the SEC and served as senior policy advisor to Commissioner Allison Lee before joining Kohn, Kohn and Colapinto, is a big proponent of whistleblowers hiring lawyers and describes counsel's job as a three-phase campaign: getting the information in a form the SEC understands, working with staff through the investigation, then advocating for the best award possible [wsT0MJ2Q9Gg @ 00:18:36]. Mahany Law ties this directly to the odds, noting the SEC issues awards on less than 1 percent of tips, which is why the firm brought on the SEC's former chief of investigations to make sure its claims get attention [PTeabZ29k14 @ 00:01:05].

On protection, practitioners converge on one blunt rule: report to the SEC, not just the hotline. Zuckerman Law explains that the Dodd-Frank anti-retaliation provision covers an internal disclosure only when the whistleblower has also reported the potential securities violation to the SEC, while Sarbanes-Oxley protects internal reports and authorizes uncapped damages for emotional distress and reputational harm [EG1qQyQJKzg @ 00:01:08]. Feller traces the cutoff to the Supreme Court's Digital Realty ruling and says that when a corporate insider calls weighing whether to go to a manager or the SEC, the advice is to report to the SEC, because the rules as written give no retaliation protection otherwise [wsT0MJ2Q9Gg @ 00:34:53]. Sean McKessy, the first chief of the SEC whistleblower office and now a partner at Phillips & Cohen, calls the 9-0 decision the product of a drafting error nobody intended, but says counsel now has to warn clients who want to report internally that they may be forfeiting enhanced protections, including two and a half times back pay instead of one times and a private right of action straight to court [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 00:44:28]. Brown goes further, warning against internal compliance lines entirely because the company will try to pin it on you and fire you [b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:07:53].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Execution starts with Form TCR, and Hall T. Martin's Startup Funding Espresso flags that some SEC claims must be filed within 3 years of the act of fraud, so the faster the claim goes in, the better the odds [ut1fgqxQy-M @ 00:00:38]. The internal-report clock is 120 days: Parnham and Associates says an employee who reports through the company's compliance program stays eligible as long as the SEC tip lands within 120 days, and that participating in the internal program actually pushes the award toward the 30 percent end, while frustrating it, skipping it, or taking part in the fraud drags the number down or cuts you out [8tuRViP_j4Y @ 00:02:57]. The same 120-day window applies after reporting to another agency first; Wiley Rein walks through a $2.2 million award, the first ever paid to someone who went elsewhere before the SEC, with the agency crediting the case opening the referral would have caused [lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:06:51]. Brown sees the opposite pattern burn people: insiders who cooperate with the DOJ, a US attorney's office or the FBI for years, then read about a settlement in the hundreds of millions and call a lawyer, may already be too late without a properly filed TCR [b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:01:14].

Once the tip is in, the award number rides a sliding scale that Brown says can seem arbitrary but can be argued. The listed factors: how transparent and cooperative you were, how incisive the information was, whether you were an insider who intimately revealed the scandal or an outsider who cobbled together a theory, and even how responsive your counsel was [b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:01:46]. Wiley Rein reads the SEC's own highlighted awards, a $4 million overseas award, the $2.2 million referral award and a $1 million outsider award backed by substantial corroborating documentation, as one repeated message: the more assistance you provide through the investigation, the more likely you get paid [lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:07:58]. Ehrman lays out the two entry doors: causing the agency to open an investigation, a much lower threshold, or significantly contributing to one already running, where several whistleblowers can each collect and split the 10 to 30 percent, and the CFTC has paid multiple claimants who each supplied different information on one matter [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 01:01:41]. Feller adds the machinery behind the check: the Office of the Whistleblower processes award applications and makes the preliminary determination of the amount, and the five commissioners vote the final award [wsT0MJ2Q9Gg @ 00:14:54].

The scoreboard numbers explain both the gold rush and the denial pile. Wiley Rein's Maddie Cohen pulled the fiscal 2018 report: 5,282 tips, a number that grew every year since 2012, and $168 million awarded that year, including $83 million to three individuals and $54 million to two, against $326 million to 59 awardees since inception [lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:04:37]. Mahany Law points to March 2018, when the SEC awarded $50 million in one case and $33 million in another on the same day [PTeabZ29k14 @ 00:00:24]. McKessy, who built the office from scratch, counts 6,900 tips in fiscal 2020, more than 40,000 since August 2011, and 153 people paid a combined $816 million [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 00:14:51]. Brown brings it to fiscal 2023: over 18,000 tips, nearly $600 million paid to just 68 individuals, including a record $279 million to one whistleblower, which works out to one award for every 265 tips, followed by 31 straight denials that Brown prices at one-in-2.1-billion coin-flip odds, and Brown, LLC's own anonymous client sits inside that streak, litigating in circuit court over a $100 million Ernst & Young action the SEC ostensibly concedes rested on the tip [0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:03:54].

callout.title: Moves the SEC Whistleblower Bar Uses to Get Paid
callout.body: Four plays the practitioners run to keep a tip alive from intake through the award vote.
items: Police the notice of covered action yourself: the SEC may settle on your information without telling you, so check its site regularly and file the award claim on time [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:02:25].

Back-channel the agency before betting on a crowded matter: McKessy called a unit head about a cyber target and a couple of days later got an SEC New York office email asking for the information [Phillips & Cohen LLP — j2GyHTrfNTE @ 01:03:48].

Treat the tip as a proactive defense: an insider who first alerted the authorities holds a chip if the hammer comes down and the matter turns criminal [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — UJOLP8WkFPo @ 00:02:04].
Package the evidence so it makes the SEC's job easier; well-packaged information plus substantial assistance is what rises to the top of thousands of tips [Wiley Rein LLP — lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:13:52].

sop_steps.title: Lock the route before touching internal channels
sop_steps.action: Talk to SEC whistleblower counsel before using any company compliance line or hotline.
sop_steps.detail: Brown warns internal compliance lines let the company pin it on you and fire you, leaving all downside and none of the upside, and Digital Realty ties Dodd-Frank retaliation protection to an SEC report [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:07:53].

sop_steps.title: File the TCR anonymously through counsel
sop_steps.action: Submit Form TCR through your attorney, drafted so the SEC grasps the significance on first read.
sop_steps.detail: Anonymous reporters stay eligible for a monetary award only if the tip comes through an attorney, and a poorly drafted tip may never clear the initial screen [Parnham and Associates — 8tuRViP_j4Y @ 00:04:16].

sop_steps.title: Feed the investigation with ongoing assistance
sop_steps.action: Keep supplying documents, corroboration, and answers to staff throughout the investigation.
sop_steps.detail: Every award highlighted in the fiscal 2018 report credited extensive assistance throughout the investigation, a recurring theme in how the SEC sizes payouts [Wiley Rein LLP — lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:06:19].

sop_steps.title: Claim the award after the notice of covered action
sop_steps.action: Monitor the SEC site for the notice of covered action and file the award claim inside the window.
sop_steps.detail: The SEC may resolve the case on your information without telling you, and missing the timely claim alone has led to countless denials [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:02:25].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether an insider should ever touch the company hotline. Jason T. Brown of Brown, LLC, a former FBI special agent, is blunt: do not use internal compliance lines, because the company will try to pin it on you and fire you, leaving you with none of the upside and plenty of downside [b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:08:07]. Parnham and Associates teaches the opposite incentive math. Participating in the company's internal compliance program moves an award toward the 30 percent end of the 10-to-30 range, while frustrating that process, skipping it, or joining the fraud drives the award down or cuts the whistleblower out, and an internal report still preserves eligibility as long as the SEC hears within 120 days [8tuRViP_j4Y @ 00:02:57]. Andrew Feller, a 15-year SEC veteran and former senior policy advisor to Commissioner Allison Lee, sits closer to Brown. Feller calls internal reporting a plus factor for a higher award with nominally no penalty for skipping it, a structure Feller describes as a little metaphysical, but tells callers to go to the SEC because current rules deny anti-retaliation protection otherwise [wsT0MJ2Q9Gg @ 00:32:21]. The kicker, per Feller, is that it is pretty hard to know beforehand which kind of company you work for [wsT0MJ2Q9Gg @ 00:34:06].

Practitioners read the same award data in opposite directions. Brown frames the program as a near-lottery: 68 awards out of more than 18,000 tips in fiscal year 2023, fewer than four of every thousand submissions, roughly one payout per 265 tips, then 31 straight denials that Brown likens to flipping heads 31 times at odds of one in 2.1 billion, blamed on the SEC's new interpretation of technical thresholds [0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:03:54]. Sean McKessy, the first chief of the SEC whistleblower office and now a Phillips & Cohen partner, pitches durability instead: these programs are here to stay, payouts grew from about 88 million dollars when McKessy left to 816 million under the successor, and the office is now clicking on all cylinders [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 00:54:14]. Feller lands in between, insisting very smart people inside the agency take tips very seriously while conceding that nothing may happen as a result for a variety of reasons [wsT0MJ2Q9Gg @ 00:17:42]. Mahany Law sells the intake as a simple three-step process of investigation, SEC inquiry, and a fight for the largest award, yet pegs awards at less than 1 percent of tips received, which it uses to justify hiring a former SEC chief of investigations [PTeabZ29k14 @ 00:00:46].

A third fault line is whose information is award-grade. Brown ranks the intimate insider who reveals the details of a scandal far above an outsider who merely postulated and cobbled together a theory, calling the two much different utility and much different worth on a sliding scale that may seem arbitrary but can be argued [b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:01:46]. Chris Ehrman, director of the CFTC whistleblower office since 2013, frames it from the agency side: the independent-analysis prong of original information brings the program closer to qui tam than it gets credit for, because outside trading experts who watch the market daily can take staff by the hand on possible spoofing that agency surveillance misses [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 00:27:48]. Scott Silver of Silver Law Group likewise counts a current employee, a victim of an investment scheme, or an outside analyst who voluntarily provides new information as eligible, and calls submitting through a securities whistleblower attorney possible and often advisable [AoceOfN67y8 @ 00:00:48]. Wiley Rein's review of fiscal 2018 backs the outsider lane with a $1 million award to a company outsider who supplied new information plus substantial corroborating documentation of a violation by a registered entity that hit retail investors [lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:07:40].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common self-inflicted loss is procedural, not substantive. Brown warns that the SEC may settle a matter built on your information and never tell you, so the whistleblower has to find the Notice of Covered Action by checking the SEC site regularly and file a timely claim after the action goes public; missing that step alone has produced countless denials [0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:02:25]. The second trap is the wrong door. Brown describes insiders who go straight to the Department of Justice, a U.S. attorney's office, or the FBI, cooperate for years, read that the company was busted for hundreds of millions, and only then call a whistleblower firm, which may be too late because no TCR was filed the right way [b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:01:14]. Wiley Rein flags the narrow escape hatch: in April 2018 the SEC paid its first award, $2.2 million, to someone who reported to another agency first, under a rule allowing 120 days to bring the same information to the SEC [lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:06:51]. Hall Martin layers on the outer clock: most claims must be filed within 10 years of the fraud, some IRS and SEC claims within 3 years, and the faster the submission, the better the chance of success [ut1fgqxQy-M @ 00:00:38].

The second failure mode is bringing the SEC something it already has, and there is no foolproof way to know in advance. McKessy admits to collecting a couple of award denials where enforcement staff said everything the client provided was great but already in the investigative file, which McKessy calls frustrating and unknowable at intake; the countermeasure McKessy used was calling the relevant unit head, in one case the cyber unit, and watching a New York office staffer email days later asking for the material [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 01:03:48]. Phillips & Cohen's Erica Kelton adds that vetting is brutal on the practitioner side, with only about three to five percent of inquiries turning into SEC or CFTC submissions [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 00:38:17]. Wiley Rein warns that thousands of tips mean whistleblowers who want to stand out need well packaged information that makes the SEC's job easier, usually backed by substantial assistance through the investigation [lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:14:06]. Brown goes further, saying a poorly drafted tip that lacks legal framing may bore the examiner after a sentence or two and land in the government circular file, the trash, like the bulk of the 18,000 tips did [0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:07:03].

The third trap is assuming protection that does not exist. Feller recounts that the Digital Realty plaintiff, an internal whistleblower who reported through a hotline, was demoted and fired, and believed Dodd-Frank anti-retaliation protection applied, only for the Supreme Court to rule that it covers only those who reported to the SEC [wsT0MJ2Q9Gg @ 00:27:21]. Zuckerman Whistleblower Law Firm draws the same line: the Dodd-Frank provision protects an internal disclosure only where the whistleblower has also reported a potential violation to the SEC, while Sarbanes-Oxley covers internal reports and authorizes uncapped damages for emotional distress and reputational harm, with critical differences in statute of limitations and exhaustion requirements [EG1qQyQJKzg @ 00:01:25]. Wiley Rein shows what retaliation looks like on the ground: the day after Paradigm Capital Management's head trader disclosed an SEC report, the firm stripped trading and supervisory duties, cut email and network access, and marginalized the trader into resigning, ultimately paying $1.7 million in disgorgement plus a $300,000 civil penalty for fraud and retaliation [lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:11:13]. McKessy flags the contract trap: severance agreements that literally barred reporting to the Office of the Whistleblower, or required telling the general counsel first, which destroys confidentiality and anonymity [j2GyHTrfNTE @ 00:46:44].

callout.title: Four Checks Before a TCR Goes Out
callout.body: Each gate below maps to a loss a practitioner reported firsthand: a missed claim window, a wrong-agency filing, an internal report with no protection behind it, or an identity that surfaced later.
items: Calendar a recurring check of SEC Notice of Covered Action postings and file the award claim inside the window, because the SEC may settle off your tip without telling you [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:02:25].

File the TCR the right way before or alongside any DOJ, U.S. attorney, or FBI cooperation, since years of cooperation without a TCR may leave the claim too late [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:01:14].

If a report already went to a hotline or supervisor, get the same information to the SEC within 120 days to keep eligibility and Dodd-Frank retaliation coverage [Parnham and Associates — 8tuRViP_j4Y @ 00:02:57].
Price in identity risk: anonymity runs through an attorney, but if the case goes to court or turns criminal the whistleblower's name may have to surface [Wiley Rein LLP — lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:04:01].

chapters.pull_quote: Good information isn't always enough. You have to present it the right way at the right time and through the right channels. — Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm (0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:02:43).
action_checklist: Have the submission structured with legal framing and the markers the SEC expects before filing, so it survives the initial screen instead of landing in the circular file [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:06:45].

File the TCR through an SEC whistleblower lawyer to stay anonymous from start to finish, since a solo filer cannot remain anonymous [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — b9I9BCtPjzw @ 00:03:15].
Package the information so it makes the SEC's job easier and commit to substantial assistance throughout the investigation to rise to the top of the heap [Wiley Rein LLP — lzz_1rNcrwk @ 00:14:06].
Test whether the SEC is already working the matter by having counsel call the relevant unit head, then direct the material to the staff who respond [Phillips & Cohen LLP — j2GyHTrfNTE @ 01:03:48].

Monitor SEC Notice of Covered Action postings regularly and file a timely claim once the action is public, even if the SEC never contacts you [Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm — 0_sJP-wJPRc @ 00:02:25].

Map retaliation exposure under both Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank, including the differences in statute of limitations and exhaustion of administrative remedies, before acting [Zuckerman Whistleblower Law Firm — EG1qQyQJKzg @ 00:01:42].

chapters.question_prompt: What anti-retaliation protections exist for financial whistleblowers, and how do the CFTC, AML/FinCEN, DOJ, and Treasury reward programs pay tipsters?
chapters.title: Dodd-Frank Protections and the Expanding Financial Bounty Programs
chapters.subtitle: SOX and Dodd-Frank anti-retaliation, the SEC's first retaliation action, CFTC derivatives-fraud rewards, AML/sanctions whistleblower awards and FinCEN's proposed rules, DOJ's corporate whistleblower incentive pilot, and Treasury's $30,000 tip rewards
chapters.executive_summary: Bounty lawyers, former agency insiders and defense counsel converge on one formula. Voluntary, original information that leads to more than $1 million in sanctions pays 10 to 30 percent across the SEC, CFTC and AML programs, and related-action awards stack on top. CFTC whistleblower office director Raagnee Beri reports that roughly 42 percent of FY2024 CFTC enforcement matters involved whistleblowers. The street mechanics turn on clocks and channels: a 120-day window for compliance staff, Sarbanes-Oxley's 180-day retaliation deadline versus Dodd-Frank's six years, anonymity only through counsel, and a FinCEN maximum-award presumption proposed at $15 million. Newer lanes include DOJ's tiered pilot and Treasury's flat $30,000 fraud portal. Practitioners split on reporting internally first, on company counter-incentives, on Treasury's discretionary payouts, and on FinCEN's confidentiality and bankruptcy loopholes.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The payout math is the one thing every bounty lawyer on the circuit repeats without variation. Whistleblowers International pitches the CFTC program as paying anywhere between 10 and 30 percent of whatever the government collects off a tipster's information. The collections must exceed $1 million [nGZvKSKSh-Y @ 00:01:48]. Chris Erman of Phillips & Cohen is the former director of the CFTC whistleblower office and a 14-year veteran of SEC enforcement. Erman adds the related-action kicker: if a second agency brings a successful case on the same information, the tipster is eligible for another 10 to 30 percent of that agency's sanctions [dyn9ni2HPDU @ 00:00:23]. Foley & Lardner's Ken Weiner traces the SEC side to Section 21F of the Exchange Act. Dodd-Frank added that section in July 2010, and it forces the SEC to pay awards on voluntary, original information that leads to collections of at least $1 million [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:14:27]. Robert Eckard maps the same 10-to-30-percent band onto the money-laundering program. There, Treasury pays on collected sanctions from Bank Secrecy Act actions exceeding $1 million [tLBsvqESK6o @ 00:01:51]. Four separate shops give one formula: original tip, million-dollar floor, ten-to-thirty cut.

The second point of agreement is that the money dies on paperwork. Whistleblowers International tells tipsters to file a Form TCR (tip, complaint or referral) and to strictly follow every CFTC filing procedure. Mistakes lead to a denial of the reward [nGZvKSKSh-Y @ 00:02:08]. Brian Mahany of Mahany Law is blunter. His firm constantly hears from people who wrote a letter to an agency or called a hotline and never got paid. If you fail to follow the procedural rules, there are no rewards and no exceptions [BueLAsaxhHM @ 00:03:40]. The asset being sold is original information. Weiner breaks the SEC definition into three tests: the information must come from independent knowledge or independent analysis, must not already be known to the SEC, and must not come exclusively from public sources [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:18:34]. Tony Munter frames what the tipster actually gets. In a False Claims Act qui tam, the relator stands in the government's shoes and files in court. The SEC program gives no independent right of action: you hand the agency a tip, the Commission decides whether to pursue it, and the harm runs to defrauded investors rather than the government [tW8oVBiMkLg @ 00:00:45]. Packaging the tip is the whole game.

Anonymity runs through counsel, and the bar agrees on that structure. Whistleblowers International says the CFTC grants anonymity to whistleblowers represented by a lawyer [nGZvKSKSh-Y @ 00:02:56]. Eckard confirms that a represented AML tipster may submit anonymously to FinCEN. Treasury and DOJ staff are barred from disclosing information that could reasonably reveal the tipster's identity, except to a defendant in a public proceeding [tLBsvqESK6o @ 00:04:13]. Poppy Alexander of Whistleblower Partners explains why counsel is required. Lawyers carry ethical obligations and certify to the agency that the filer is who they say they are. That certification is a backstop against AI-generated spam, stolen identities, and filers who think they know more than they do [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:33:47]. On retaliation, the Garrison, Levin-Epstein team draws the baseline every employee needs. Sarbanes-Oxley protects internal reports to a supervisor or compliance department under a contributing-factor standard. Dodd-Frank protection attaches only when the concern goes directly to the SEC, and reporting internally to a manager or compliance is not enough [ft81gWsFd2M @ 00:02:02]. The consensus prerequisite is sequencing: get counsel, pick the reporting channel deliberately, and only then move. The Garrison team warns that early choices about who to report to and when decide which protections attach.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Timing is where the money is won or lost, and the clocks are specific. Weiner walks through the SEC carve-out for compliance officers. People whose principal duties are compliance or internal audit are normally excluded from awards. Once 120 days have passed since a supervisor, the chief compliance officer, the chief legal officer or the audit committee received the information, they are free to go to the SEC and stay bounty-eligible [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:23:52]. A second clock protects internal reporters. If an employee reports through company channels and contacts the SEC within 120 days, the SEC credits the employee when the company later hands over the same information or its investigation results [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:25:13]. Weiner also reports what the plaintiff side actually tells clients. On a substantial issue, most whistleblower attorneys would not advise reporting to the company first, though some advise reporting internally and to the SEC at the same time [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:27:50]. The retaliation clocks run differently. Sarbanes-Oxley gives only 180 days from the retaliation to file. Dodd-Frank allows up to six years and potentially double damages, but only if the report went directly to the SEC [ft81gWsFd2M @ 00:01:32].

The money-laundering lane has been rebuilt from scratch. Mahany notes that the old Bank Secrecy Act rewards were capped at $150,000 and were completely discretionary, which is why very few AML rewards were ever paid [BueLAsaxhHM @ 00:00:40]. Eckard lays out the fix. The Anti-Money Laundering Whistleblower Improvement Act, signed December 23, 2022, sets a 10 percent minimum award. It extends coverage to sanctions violations under IEEPA, the Trading with the Enemy Act and the Kingpin Act. It also expressly lets compliance and audit staff and non-US citizens collect [tLBsvqESK6o @ 00:01:15]. Poppy Alexander describes how FinCEN routes tips. They arrive by email or online form and get farmed out to OFAC for sanctions, to the OCC and Federal Reserve for bank issues, and to DOJ. FinCEN's whistleblower office still controls the award, so the tipster must keep FinCEN informed of every conversation with OFAC or anyone else [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:21:08]. Andrew Feller adds the speed lever. FinCEN proposed a presumption of the maximum 30 percent award with a $15 million threshold, against $5 million at the SEC. The CFTC estimated that roughly 80 percent of its historic awards would have qualified under its own similar proposal [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:12:18].

The newest bounty lanes stack on top. Matt Kelly explains that the DOJ Criminal Division pilot pays up to 30 percent of net proceeds after asset forfeiture. In his example, a $300 million settlement with $100 million going to victim restitution leaves the tipster's 30 percent calculated on the remaining $200 million [bFRmUwE-_F4 @ 00:01:27]. Tom Fox flags the tiers: 30 percent of the first $100 million, 5 percent of anything between $100 million and $500 million, and nothing clear above that. The pilot is scheduled to run three years [bFRmUwE-_F4 @ 00:18:25]. Kelly also names the targets: FEPA bribery of foreign officials, FCPA cases at non-public companies outside SEC reach, and health care fraud. These are the gaps where no awards program existed before [bFRmUwE-_F4 @ 00:02:07]. At the retail end, Treasury Secretary Bessent announced a $25 million fraud whistleblower incentive fund. It offers a $30,000 reward for information leading to a conviction or enforcement action, submitted through a single centralized portal at america.gov/fraud that replaces scattered agency tip lines [FnUiQJNaMn8 @ 00:04:10]. The spread is enormous: one lane pays a flat $30,000, while the others pay percentages of nine-figure settlements.

callout.title: How the bounty bar actually packages a winning tip
callout.body: Former agency insiders and whistleblower counsel converge on curation, proof of what leadership knew, contemporaneous notes, and sustained cooperation as the levers that move an award.
items: Do not dump terabytes on the agency. The government wants the good material, and anything potentially attorney-client privileged should be held back until a taint process or segregation is set up, because it can taint the whole investigative team [Fraud in America — R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:31:26].

Point FinCEN at data it already holds. Banks self-report so much that the agency often lacks only the key showing where to look, and showing that senior leadership knew about the problem is what tipsters most often leave out [Fraud in America — R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:14:54].

Write down what you saw and when, and talk to an employment lawyer before making the whistleblower complaint. Early choices about who to report to and when dictate which protections apply [Garrison, Levin-Epstein, Fitzgerald & Pirrotti — ft81gWsFd2M @ 00:02:17].

Keep feeding the agency after the first tip. In a $37 million SEC award, the whistleblower's ongoing, extensive and timely assistance exposed the full context that the company's own self-disclosure left out [Compliance Podcast Network — bFRmUwE-_F4 @ 00:14:00].

sop_steps.title: Lock the record and retain counsel
sop_steps.action: Write down what was seen and when, then retain whistleblower or employment counsel before any report goes out.
sop_steps.detail: The Garrison team tells employees to document what they saw and when and to talk to an employment lawyer before the complaint [Garrison, Levin-Epstein, Fitzgerald & Pirrotti — ft81gWsFd2M @ 00:02:17]. Counsel also unlocks anonymous filing at the CFTC [Whistleblowers International — nGZvKSKSh-Y @ 00:02:56].

sop_steps.title: Pick the channel and start the clocks
sop_steps.action: Decide between internal, direct-to-agency or simultaneous reporting, and calendar the 120-day and retaliation deadlines.
sop_steps.detail: Compliance staff become eligible 120 days after leadership receives the information, and internal reporters keep credit if they reach the SEC within 120 days. Most whistleblower attorneys skip reporting internally first on substantial issues [Foley & Lardner LLP — 7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:27:50].

sop_steps.title: File the formal tip with a curated package
sop_steps.action: Submit through the formal channel (Form TCR, or FinCEN's email address or online form) with targeted evidence rather than a data dump.
sop_steps.detail: Whistleblowers need to file a Form TCR and strictly follow the CFTC's filing procedures, because mistakes lead to denial of the reward [Whistleblowers International — nGZvKSKSh-Y @ 00:02:08]. Privileged material is held back until a taint process exists [Fraud in America — R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:31:26].

sop_steps.title: Cooperate, keep the award office informed, then claim
sop_steps.action: Assist every agency that picks up the tip, keep the award office informed of each contact, and file the award submission after the enforcement action.
sop_steps.detail: After an enforcement action, the whistleblower submits an award claim to FinCEN, which manages the award even when OFAC or other agencies ran the case, so the tipster keeps FinCEN informed of every contact [Fraud in America — R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:22:24].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over where the first report goes. Josh at Garrison, Levin-Epstein lays out the fork: Sarbanes-Oxley protects a purely internal report to a supervisor or compliance department, but the employee gets only 180 days to file a retaliation complaint, while Dodd-Frank offers more damages, potentially double, and a six-year window, yet only kicks in when the concern goes directly to the SEC [ft81gWsFd2M @ 00:01:32]. Ken Weiner at Foley & Lardner reports that most whistleblower attorneys he talks to would not advise a client sitting on a substantial issue to tell the company before the SEC, though some would advise reporting to both simultaneously [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:27:50]. Tom Fox and Matt Kelly argue internal reporting is far from dead: Fox puts the share of SEC whistleblowers who reported internally first at 85 to 90 percent, and Kelly says a solid majority of employees want to report inside because they want the company to do well [bFRmUwE-_F4 @ 00:10:39]. Andrew Feller calls FinCEN's proposed handling of internal reporting a mixed bag, flagging the operator reality that the internal mechanism may be flawed or the person receiving the report may be complicit in the wrongdoing [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:17:20].

Steve Pearlman and Ruben Guttman go head to head on what bounties do to the workforce. Pearlman expects two types of whistleblowers to come out of the woodwork: the private-attorney-general type acting in good faith with religious zeal, and the disgruntled employee who sees the writing on the wall, holds dirt on a supervisor, and wants leverage for a sweeter deal or a richer severance package [eSiH7Rgnhe4 @ 00:03:30]. Pearlman reports companies responding by developing mechanisms to compete with the 10 to 30 percent bounties, some trying to monetize an incentive to keep the complaint internal and others enhancing performance evaluations for good-faith fraud reduction [eSiH7Rgnhe4 @ 00:05:40]. Guttman calls that a stunning admission, arguing that where a company like Pfizer went through three integrity agreements and kept violating the law, or an Enron-style situation, there is no viable internal compliance program to work with, so the call is case by case [eSiH7Rgnhe4 @ 00:06:47]. On the corporate defense side, Lisa Noler at Foley tells companies to use the internal investigation to build a credibility file on the whistleblower, the government's primary witness, and to tell prosecutors the witness will get killed on cross-examination [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:38:27].

The program rulebooks themselves split on who gets paid and how. Ken Weiner walks through the SEC's exclusion of employees whose principal duties involve compliance or internal audit, escapable mainly through a time exception: once 120 days have passed since the supervisor, chief compliance officer, chief legal officer, or audit committee received the information, the compliance official is free to go to the SEC and stay bounty-eligible [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:23:52]. Robert Eckard counters that the AMLA reward program imposes no limitation on people who learn through compliance or audit duties and expressly authorizes compliance personnel, with non-US citizens eligible too [tLBsvqESK6o @ 00:03:53]. The newest tier splits hardest. Bessent, speaking for Treasury, pitches a $25 million fund paying up to $30,000 to anyone whose information leads to a conviction or enforcement action, filed through a single portal at america.gov/fraud instead of a maze of tip lines [FnUiQJNaMn8 @ 00:04:10]. Vincent Romo's crew questions the 1 percent commission framing, notes Trump said he would personally decide who gets paid when several people claim the same tip, calls the setup subjective rather than clear-cut, and asks how many cases have actually been prosecuted after the photo ops [G7YHankdf9E @ 00:01:22].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common kill shot is procedural. Brian Mahany says his firm constantly hears from people who wrote a letter to an agency or called a hotline and never got paid, and the rule is blunt: fail the procedural rules and there are no rewards and no exceptions [BueLAsaxhHM @ 00:03:40]. Whistleblowers International gives the same warning for the CFTC: file a Form TCR, strictly follow every filing procedure, because mistakes lead to denial, and anonymity is available only to whistleblowers represented by a lawyer [nGZvKSKSh-Y @ 00:02:33]. Poppy Alexander of Whistleblower Partners attacks the FinCEN draft's demand that the first tip be certified complete, since nobody knows what complete means; the playbook is to bring the good stuff instead of terabytes, hold back anything possibly attorney-client privileged until a taint process is set up, and expect gaps when filers work without counsel, such as missing proof that the CEO knew [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:31:39]. Chris Erman of Phillips & Cohen adds the capacity constraint: the CFTC has limited resources and can only pursue a limited number of investigations, which is why packaging the information the best way possible matters [dyn9ni2HPDU @ 00:02:24].

Collection risk is the economics check most filers skip. Andrew Feller reports that the SEC does not define collected proceeds to include amounts distributed in bankruptcy, so if the company goes bankrupt before the SEC collects its sanctions, in all likelihood there is no payout, and FinCEN's draft left that same loophole open [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:24:19]. Feller warns the risk clusters in companies and industries with a higher likelihood of bankruptcy after an enforcement action, exactly the targets FinCEN should want reported, and it will get fewer of those reports unless the hole is fixed [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:25:00]. Poppy Alexander flags the million-dollar covered-action threshold: actions can be combined only if they resolve at substantially the same time, yet civil, criminal, individual, and corporate resolutions are sometimes separated by years, and she points to the SEC's approach as the fix [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:36:33]. Matt Kelly delivers the hardest number: the process is arduous and long-drawn-out at the best of times, you probably will not get $37 million, and Kelly has seen people whose careers went into the ditch collect about 800 grand six years later, not much to carry someone in their mid-40s or 50s into retirement, which is why Kelly calls this a high-risk thing people do [bFRmUwE-_F4 @ 00:17:32].

Identity exposure and evidence-gathering are where filers get burned. Sandy Wier at Foley warns that once a whistleblower is debriefed, the information becomes subject to the SEC's routine uses, including sharing with other agencies and Freedom of Information Act responses, so it is probably not going to stay confidential [7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:04:13]. Feller calls language in the FinCEN draft allowing whistleblower information to be shared with defendants to facilitate settlement one of the biggest concerns, and says if it stays in the final rule, the whistleblower bar will have very interesting conversations about whether to use the program at all [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:26:08]. The draft's disqualification for evidence obtained in violation of any state or federal law is the other trap: Poppy Alexander points to one-party versus two-party recording laws and California's civil action for illegal recordings, which gives companies an incentive to push a DA toward charges [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:28:53]. Feller cites a software engineer who left Goldman Sachs with code, not as a whistleblower, yet the firm apparently convinced New York prosecutors to bring a criminal trade secret case, showing the incentives companies have to press trade-secret and intellectual-property theories [R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:30:03].

callout.title: Four Kill Switches to Clear Before Filing
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a failure, denial, or deadline practitioners reported firsthand. Miss one and the payout or the retaliation claim can disappear.
items: Never treat a letter or hotline call as your tip; if you fail the procedural rules there are no rewards and no exceptions [Mahany Law — BueLAsaxhHM @ 00:03:59].
If you need anonymity at the CFTC, file through a lawyer, because the program ties anonymity to legal representation [Whistleblowers International — nGZvKSKSh-Y @ 00:02:56].

If you want Dodd-Frank damages and the six-year window, the report must reach the SEC directly; an internal report to a manager or compliance department is not enough [Garrison, Levin-Epstein, Fitzgerald & Pirrotti — ft81gWsFd2M @ 00:02:02].

If you went through the company's internal channel first under the SEC program, get to the SEC within 120 days to keep credit for the original information [Foley & Lardner LLP — 7vp44tFe6hs @ 00:25:52].

action_checklist: Write down what you saw and when, and talk to an employment lawyer before making the whistleblower complaint, because who you report to and when dictates which protections you keep [Garrison, Levin-Epstein, Fitzgerald & Pirrotti — ft81gWsFd2M @ 00:02:31].
File a Form TCR for CFTC matters, strictly follow every filing procedure, and confirm the government collection will exceed $1 million [Whistleblowers International — nGZvKSKSh-Y @ 00:02:08].

Track related actions by other agencies, since a CFTC whistleblower can also collect 10 to 30 percent of sanctions another agency recovers on the same information [Foundation Digital Media — dyn9ni2HPDU @ 00:00:23].

Submit the good stuff rather than terabytes, and segregate anything possibly attorney-client privileged until a taint process is worked out with the government [Fraud in America — R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:31:53].

Keep the FinCEN whistleblower office apprised of every communication with OFAC, the OCC, DOJ, or other agencies handling your tip, because FinCEN manages the award submission [Fraud in America — R3h4J-EAtro @ 00:22:54].

Stay engaged after filing: the SEC credited a $37 million award to the whistleblower's ongoing, extensive and timely assistance that exposed what the company left out [Compliance Podcast Network — bFRmUwE-_F4 @ 00:14:00].

chapters.question_prompt: How do you report tax cheats to the IRS Whistleblower Office, and what are the realistic odds, timelines, and payouts?
chapters.title: The IRS Whistleblower Program: Form 211 to Award Check
chapters.subtitle: Section 7623(b) thresholds and award percentages, Form 211 vs. Form 3949-A, a line-by-line Form 211 walkthrough, the start-to-finish process, offshore-account cases, IRS agent whistleblowers, and practitioner debate over whether the program works
chapters.executive_summary: Former IRS agents, whistleblower counsel and tax controversy litigators agree on the core deal: Form 211 is the only route to an award, payouts run 15 to 30 percent of proceeds actually collected, and nothing pays until the target exhausts every appeal. The working floor is more than $2 million in tax in dispute plus $200,000 of gross income for individual targets, but Brown says the IRS rarely moves below a likely $10 million collection. Winning files are insider-sourced, documented, current and packaged as a narrative memo with enabling-party, witness and document appendices. Timelines run seven to ten years, longer if litigated. The split: Brown and Sullivan want big splashes, while Green and Skarlatos say their billion-dollar claims never paid and the sweet spot is $10 million to $50 million of simple tax evasion.

sections.title: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who walks the program lands on the same payout math. The IRS Whistleblower Office pays 15 to 30 percent of proceeds collected and attributable to the tip, and only after the target has exhausted every appeal right and can no longer file a refund claim [i4GnKgGXiMw @ 00:01:04]. Emily Stibil of Phillips and Cohen describes that band as mandatory for eligible claims, with the final award amount set by the Whistleblower Office itself [fQss6bE5tKc @ 00:00:34]. Former IRS agent Mike Sullivan states the collection rule bluntly: if the money is not collected, the tipster does not get a nickel, so chasing a broke target is wasted time [41ejxu80Qtg @ 00:02:09]. The second point of agreement is that Form 211, the Application for Award for Original Information, is the only door to a payout, and the filing has to be right the first time. Jason T. Brown warns that calling a tip hotline or the local office, or going to the FBI or Secret Service, can get a tipster treated as a confidential informant or cooperating witness with a little cash thrown their way, but leaves zero eligibility for the real award even if the government recovers hundreds of millions [RuNrDW46nKY @ 00:01:41].

The floor numbers repeat across firms. Stibil and Brown both put the line at more than $2 million in tax, penalties, interest and additions in dispute, plus gross income above $200,000 in at least one year at issue when the target is an individual [fQss6bE5tKc @ 00:01:27]. Brown stresses that the $2 million is tax liability, not unreported income: hide $2 million of income at a roughly 50 percent effective rate and the liability is only $1 million, short of the bar. Clearing the threshold does not make a case workable. Brown says that even at $2 million the IRS is unlikely to move unless the file is blatant, well documented and likely to collect $10 million or more, against deep-pocketed targets with collectible assets, willful conduct and a whistleblower who is an insider [tQIkb01vCTw @ 00:01:52]. Dean Zerbe of the National Whistleblower Center ranks insiders first, naming the senior bank official, the tax department and the accountant, and adds that the IRS wants conduct three years old at most for an individual and five or six for a corporation, ideally still running [O45E7FrG_mM @ 00:02:01]. Sullivan's version is that the IRS wants a whale splash that makes headlines and pleases the commissioner, not a couple of bait fish [41ejxu80Qtg @ 00:03:10].

The third consensus is that the IRS will not do the tipster's homework or forgive a thin file. Law Minded guest Alina says the IRS receives countless tips every year, so a claim built on something overheard at a restaurant is speculative, and even well-substantiated claims often go uninvestigated, which is why the firm screens out ineligible or unsupported cases before filing [sNHauc7rutQ @ 00:07:51]. A CPA, lawyer and Northeastern academic interviewed by Boston 25 says the informant essentially has to spoon-feed the dirty details, giving the IRS an idea of what taxes are missing, how it came about and what the amounts may be, so the whistleblower does all the digging [mfEL3LienPQ @ 00:01:56]. The same report estimates that 90 percent of claims are found useless and puts the reported average payout at about $224,000, because the IRS is too busy to run down every lead [mfEL3LienPQ @ 00:02:27]. Nobody sells speed either. Eric Green and Bryan Skarlatos put the average paying case at eight to ten years, and cases the IRS drags into court at twelve to twenty years minimum; Skarlatos says that, given the timeline, any new case had better be simple and easy [ruRW_hNSDYk @ 00:07:15].

sections.title: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The form itself is short; Teach Me! Personal Finance walks it as a single page split into Section A on the target and Section B on the claimant [WA3dtUQT9f8 @ 00:07:29]. Line 1 flags a new or supplemental submission, with any prior claim number entered; line 2 takes the last four digits of the target's taxpayer ID; lines 3 through 5 take the name with aliases and related taxpayers, the address and a date of birth or approximate age, and the IRS will work with partial data. Line 6 names any IRS employee previously told, line 7 checks the violation type across income, employment, employee plans, government entities and exempt organizations, line 8 states the facts and why they break the law, and line 9 explains how the information was obtained. Lines 15 and 16 lay out the tax owed by year and dollar amount, with room for at least five tax years [WA3dtUQT9f8 @ 00:12:44]. The claimant must sign personally under penalty of perjury even with a Form 2848 power of attorney on file, and the package is mailed to the Whistleblower Office [WA3dtUQT9f8 @ 00:03:53]. Alina warns that the 211 looks strikingly like a report-only form with no award, a common but devastating mix-up [sNHauc7rutQ @ 00:06:25].

The 211 is a wrapper; the winning asset is the narrative behind it. Zerbe calls the online form a check-the-box document and says the narrative is what the IRS is really reading, starting with chapter-and-verse specificity on the taxpayer and a plain-language account of the scheme [O45E7FrG_mM @ 00:09:59]. Zerbe then bolts on three sheets: an appendix of every enabling party, meaning the accounting firm and law firm helping the taxpayer; a list of who else can verify the story, where they are located and what they will likely say, preferably people the IRS can reach inside the US; and a document sheet naming each key record, who controls it and where it sits [O45E7FrG_mM @ 00:11:19]. Brown typically files a comprehensive written memo alongside the 211 walking the IRS through facts, law and documents, because the IRS wants cases silver-plattered, not a quick value meal that gets discarded [tQIkb01vCTw @ 00:06:49]. Sullivan's agent-side version is a really nice letter that someone else polishes, backed by dossiers sometimes inches thick so the reviewing agent does no work; three or four pages of he-said-she-said went straight into the garbage when Sullivan was an agent [41ejxu80Qtg @ 00:03:49].

The numbers the IRS needs are two predicate facts: what the target reported and what the true liability was. Brown's model case is a company telling the government it makes $2 million a year while the second set of books, the one hidden from the government, shows $5 million buried through sub-corporations and offshore accounts, a $3 million annual deficit stated as hard figures with the math shown, not guesswork [RuNrDW46nKY @ 00:08:47]. For a clean criminal case, Green walks the file to a local IRS Criminal Investigation special agent first, since the 211 asks whether anyone at the IRS has already seen it; one agent told Green they did not like the idea of people in Utah making the call, and CI has interviewed Green's clients [ruRW_hNSDYk @ 00:20:30]. Skarlatos agrees CI is more used to informants than the civil side, but stresses lodging the 211 before CI acts, or there is no award [ruRW_hNSDYk @ 00:22:37]. After filing, Brown reads the yearly update codes: no action means little, referred to audit is slightly promising, and referred to collections is the ding-ding-ding signal that liabilities were found [tQIkb01vCTw @ 00:08:07].
